Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 1:

(p-3501) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah Yusuf

It is named after him (Yusuf), because most of his story is mentioned in it, and most of what is in it is his story.

Al-Shihab said: When the surah before it was concluded with His words, ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers﴾ [Hud: 120], this one was mentioned after it, because it is from their news. He first mentioned what the prophets, peace be upon them, suffered from their peoples, and in this surah He mentioned what Yusuf suffered from his brothers, so that it may be known what they endured from the harm of strangers and relatives. Thus there is complete correspondence between them. The purpose is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he encountered from the harm of near and far. End of quote.

"Yusuf" is a Hebrew name; its Arabized form is Yazid, or "increase." This is because it was reported that his mother, Rahil (Rachel), had been unable to conceive for a period, and grief overcame her in the face of her co-wives who had children. When God, exalted is He, granted her, after years, a son, she named him Yusuf and said: "May my Lord give me through him another son."

This surah is Meccan by unanimous agreement, and its verses number one hundred and eleven without any disagreement.

Al-Bayhaqi reported in (al-Dala'il) that a group of the Jews, when they heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting this surah, embraced Islam because it agreed with what they had.

(p-3502) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

The discussion on the interpretation of His, exalted is He, words:

[1] ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.﴾

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾: the discussion of its like has preceded, and that they are either letters listed in the manner of enumeration. The indication in His words ﴿These are the verses of the clear Book﴾ refers to the verses of the surah; what follows is treated as what precedes, since it is anticipated. The use of the distant demonstrative is for its greatness and the remoteness of its rank. Alternatively, it is a name for the surah, and the demonstrative "these" refers to it. By "the Book" is meant the surah, since it has the meaning of "the written," so it is applied to it. Or it means the Qur'an, since just as it is applied to all of it, it is applied to part of it. And "al-Mubin" (the clear) means that its matter and its inimitability are manifest, if it is taken from "bana" intransitively meaning "appeared." If it is taken from the transitive form, then the object is implied, i.e., that it is from Allah, exalted is He.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have sent it down﴾, that is, the Book described by what has been mentioned, ﴿as an Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand﴾, meaning: so that you may comprehend it, grasp its meanings, and it may not be confused for you. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had We made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained in detail?"﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. Or: ﴿that you may use your intellects﴾ in it, so that you know that its narration of stories in this manner, from one who had not learned tales, is miraculous and cannot occur except by revelation. Or: ﴿that you may understand﴾ by its being sent down in Arabic the meanings and secrets it contains, which other languages do not contain or bear. This is because the language of the Arabs is the most eloquent of languages, the clearest, the broadest, and the most capable of conveying the meanings that subsist in souls (p-3503). Some of them said: He sent down the noblest of Books, in the noblest of languages, upon the noblest of Messengers, through the mediation of the noblest of angels, and this took place in the noblest of places on earth and in the noblest of months of the year, which is Ramadan; thus nobility was perfected for it in every respect.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[3] ﴿We relate to you the best of stories, by Our revealing to you this Qur'an, though you were before it certainly among the unaware.﴾

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, i.e., the most original in its manner, the most wondrous in its style, the most truthful in its reports, and the most comprehensive in its wisdoms and lessons. ﴿by Our revealing to you﴾, i.e., by Our inspiring to you ﴿this Qur'an, though you were before it certainly among the unaware﴾, i.e., of it, it had not occurred to your mind. The expression of lack of knowledge as heedlessness is to honor the status of the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been permitted in this that it be the object of "naqussu" (we relate), with "ahsana" (best) being in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar); and that it be the object of "awhayna" (We revealed), with the object of "naqussu" being "ahsana" or being omitted; and that it be a substitute (badal) for "ma" (what), on the basis that it is a relative pronoun (mawsula), or a predicate omitted in the same way.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[4] ﴿When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾

﴿When Joseph said to his father﴾ meaning Ya'qub (Jacob) son of Ishaq (Isaac) son of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him. The temporal clause (al-zarf) is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the object before it, or it is an object of an elided verb. ﴿O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.﴾ Joseph only confided to his father with this dream, because he believed in his father's complete knowledge and his compassion for him, to the extent that if the dream were to displease him, he could have turned it away from him.

Al-Qashani said: This is one of the dreams that require interpretation, due to the imaginative faculty moving from the noble souls, the one which presented to the soul, from the unseen, their prostration to him, to the stars, the sun, and the moon, while in reality they were none other than his parents and his brothers. (يا أبَتِ) its original form is يا أبِي, so the ta' of feminine marking was substituted for the ya', because of their similarity in being added. Its vowel is kasra because it is a substitute for a letter that corresponds to it. It has also been read with a fatha, because that is the vowel of its original form, or because it was originally (يا أبَتا), so the alif was dropped and the fatha remained. It has also been read with a damma, treating it as one of the feminine nouns ending in ta', without considering the substitution.

His words (رَأيْتُهُمُ) are a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining the condition in which he saw them, so there is no repetition. Or it is an emphasis of the first statement, to refresh it given the lapse of time, as in His words: ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35]. The pronoun for them was treated as that of rational beings and their attribute was made into a sound masculine plural, because they were described with an attribute of rational beings, which is prostration.

Al-Mahayimi said: If it is valid that they were speaking, then there is no difficulty. He said: I have not seen anyone address the manner of the prostration, and perhaps it is the moving of their upper side toward the lower, whether they appeared rounded or elongated. End of quote.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[5] ﴿He said, "My dear son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾

﴿He said, "My dear son"﴾ He diminished him (with the diminutive "bunayy") because of his young age, out of compassion for him, and because of the sweetness of the diminutive form. ﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme﴾ meaning, lest they act on your account, or to destroy you, with a great and destructive stratagem against you. ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾ meaning, manifest in enmity, so he spares no effort in leading your brothers astray and driving them toward what holds no good.

Al-Qashani said: This prohibition is among the general inspirations. The image of the unseen may appear from the immaterial spiritual realities to the soul, and its effect reaches the heart without being individually specified in the self, until knowledge of it occurs as it is. Thus fear and wariness arise in the self from it if it is disliked, and joy and delight if it is desired. This kind of inspiration is called warnings and glad tidings. So he (peace be upon him) feared, before its occurrence, what would befall him, and therefore forbade him to tell them of his dream as a precaution. It is also possible that his caution came from the dream's indication of his nobility and honor and the increase of his rank over his brothers, so he feared their envy of him when they became aware of this. End.

**Note:**

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): Al-Kiya said: This indicates the permissibility of withholding the display of a blessing from one who is feared to envy it and to harbor ill will.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: In it is a judgment by custom that brothers and relatives envy one another. He said: In it is also that Ya'qub knew the interpretation of the dream and did not mind it, for a man wishes his son to be better than himself, but a brother does not wish that for his brother.

Some of the Yemeni exegetes said: Al-Hakim said: This indicates that in some circumstances it is obligatory to conceal a virtue, as a safeguard against the envious. This falls under our saying: If a good thing becomes a cause of something ugly, it becomes ugly. From it is the verse of al-An'am: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 108].

In this regard is what is related from Zayn al-'Abidin:

*Indeed I conceal from my knowledge its gems, lest one ignorant who sees the truth should tempt us.*

These are the well-known verses, which al-Ghazali in (Minhaj al-'Abidin) and al-Daylami in the book (al-Tasfiyah) related from Zayn al-'Abidin. And this is Ya'qub, may the blessings of God be upon him, commanding Yusuf, peace be upon him, not to relate his dream to his brothers, and the meaning is one. So there is no sense in the objection of one who denies this and claims that knowledge may not be concealed. End.

Its intent is that the fear of the evil of wicked people is among the obstacles that turn one away from proclaiming the truth.

(p-3506) Al-Sayyid Ibn al-Murtada al-Yamani said in (Iythar al-Haqq): Among what has increased the truth's obscurity and concealment is the fear of the knowers, despite their small number, of the scholars of evil, the sultans of injustice, and the devils of mankind, together with the permissibility of taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation) in such circumstances, by the explicit text of the Qur'an and the consensus (ijma') of the people of Islam. Fear has never ceased to prevent the manifestation of truth, and the one upholding the truth has never ceased to be an enemy to most of mankind.

He, may God have mercy on him, had earlier mentioned, in arguing for taqiyya, that God, exalted is He, praised the believer of Pharaoh's household while he concealed his faith, and the surah of (al-Mu'min) was named after him. It is also authentically reported that 'Ammar was commanded to it and it was approved for him, and the verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿Except one who is compelled while his heart is secure in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. It is authentically reported from Abu Hurayra that he said, in that early era: "I memorized from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) two receptacles. As for one of them, I have spread it among you; and as for the other, if I spread it, this throat would be cut." Al-Ghazali said in the introduction to (al-Maqsad al-Asna): Whoever mixes with people is bound to avoid them. But for one who has perceived the truth, it is difficult for him to feign blindness. End.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 6 (part 1 of 2)**

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[6] ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you, and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Ya'qub, just as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq. Indeed your Lord is Knowing, Wise.﴾

﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾ means: like that choosing, by showing you this momentous dream, He will select you for prophethood and leadership. ﴿And teach you the interpretation of events﴾ means the interpretation of dreams (ta'bir al-manamat). The interpretation was called ta'wil (interpretation, literally "returning something to its origin") because it makes the thing seen return to and become what the interpreter mentions as the meaning of the dream. Al-ahadith is the plural-form noun of hadith (event, report), and dreams were named by it because they are either a "speech" from an angel, from the soul, or from a devil. ﴿And complete His favor upon you﴾ means through what your affair will ultimately come to. ﴿Upon the family of Ya'qub﴾ means his household among his sons and their entourage; that is, He will shower His favor upon them through you. ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq. Indeed your Lord is Knowing﴾ of who deserves being chosen ﴿Wise﴾ in His creation.

**Notes:**

**First:** Abu al-Su'ud said: It seems that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, by his saying ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾ was alluding to what would happen with Yusuf, peace be upon him, namely his interpreting the dreams of the two companions of the prison and the dream of the king, and that this would be a means toward the great leadership that God would bring him to, which he expressed by "completing the favor." Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this from Yusuf through revelation. Or he meant that this quality would be a cause for the manifestation of his affair, peace be upon him, in general. In that case, his knowledge could come through firasa (discernment, physiognomic insight), and inference from signs, proofs, indications and tokens, that whoever God has enabled to receive such a dream must also be enabled to interpret it and the like, and to distinguish what is external (afaqi) from what is internal (anfusi). How could it not be so, when such a dream indicates the perfection of his soul's ability in the world of images ('alam al-mithal), and the strength of its activities therein? Thus he would be more receptive to the outpouring of knowledge related to that world, and to what it reflects of matters that occur in accordance with it in the world of witnessing (alam al-shahadah), and stronger in grasping the relations between the perceived forms in one of those two worlds and the existing things that appear in conformity with them in the other world. This wondrous affair must necessarily be a model for the manifestation of the affair of whoever is characterized by it, and a basis for the operation of his rulings. For every prophet, peace and blessings be upon them all, has a miracle through which his effects appear and his rulings take effect.

**Second:** The verse has been used as evidence that the grandfather (al-jadd) may be called "father" (al-ab). Thus it indicates that whoever attributes a man to his grandfather and says "O son of So-and-so," it is not slander (qadhf).

**Third:** Al-Mahayimi said: Among the benefits of this passage are: the recommendation of keeping a secret; the permissibility of warning against a specific person; praising a person to his face when it will not harm him; considering the cause even if it does not have an effect; that every event has an interpretation according to the friends of God (awliya'); and that dreams are interpreted even when they come from the world of imagination (al-khayal). For the imagination (al-mukhayyilah) forms intelligible meanings in sensible images, and sends them to the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak), so it perceives them. The true ones among them occur through the soul's connection when it is free, even minimally, from managing the body. It is then imagined with what it contains that corresponds to the meanings. If the correspondence is very strong, it needs no interpretation; otherwise it needs it. So the reports of this dream are a sign, and of what followed from it, signs.

**Discussion on Dreams**

The Imam al-Raghib al-Isfahani said in his book al-Dhari'ah, in the section on firasa, something to this effect:

Among firasa is the knowledge of dreams. God, exalted be He, has magnified their matter in all the revealed books, and said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾ [al-Isra' 60], and He said: ﴿When God showed them to you in your sleep﴾ [al-Anfal 43], and in the story of Ibrahim: ﴿O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾ [al-Saffat 102], and His saying: ﴿O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars﴾ [Yusuf 4].

Dreaming is an act of the rational soul; if it had no reality, this faculty in man would have no purpose, and God, exalted, is far above vanity. It is of two kinds. The first, which is the more common, is confused dreams (adghath ahlam) and the self's talk through base thoughts, because the soul in that state is like agitated water, which accepts no image.

The second, which is rarer, is sound (sahih). This is of two kinds. One kind needs no interpretation, and for this reason the interpreter needs skill to distinguish confused dreams from other dreams, and to distinguish between spiritual and bodily expressions, and to differentiate among classes of people, since among them is one whose dream is never sound and one whose dream is sound. Then among those whose dreams are sound, some are fitted to have great and weighty matters conveyed to them in sleep, and some are not. For this reason the Greeks said: the interpreter must occupy himself with interpreting the dreams of sages and kings, not of the rabble, because he has a share of prophethood. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The true dream is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood." This knowledge requires a correspondence between the one who seeks it and it. Many a wise man is not granted skill in it, and many one with little share of wisdom and the other sciences has a wondrous power in it. End.

Al-Ustadh Ibn Khaldun said: The reality of the dream is the rational soul's glance at its own spiritual essence, a flash of the forms of events. When it is spiritual, the forms of events are present in it actually, as is the case with all spiritual essences; it becomes spiritual by being stripped of corporeal matter and bodily perceptions. This sometimes happens to it as a flash through sleep, as we shall mention, and so it acquires knowledge of what it longs for of future matters, and returns with it to its faculties. If that acquisition is weak and not clear through the likeness and image in the imagination, mixed with it, then it needs interpretation for the sake of that likeness. The acquisition may be strong, dispensing with likeness, and then it needs no interpretation, since it is free of image and imagination. The cause of this flash occurring to the soul is that it is spiritual in potential, completed by the body and its faculties, until its essence becomes pure intellection and its existence is completed actually. Then it is a spiritual essence that perceives without any bodily instrument, except that its kind of spirituality is below the kind of the angels of the highest horizon, who have not completed their essences with any of the body's faculties or anything else. This readiness is present in it as long as it is in the body. Among it is a special readiness, like that of the saints (awliya'), and among it a general readiness for mankind at large, which is the matter of dreaming. As for the readiness of the prophets, it is readiness through stripping off humanity toward pure angelhood, which is the highest of spiritual things. This readiness appears in them repeatedly in states of revelation, when it inclines toward the bodily faculties, and what occurs of perception happens in them, clearly resembling the state of sleep, though the state of sleep is far lower than it. Because of this resemblance, the Lawgiver (al-Shari') described the dream as "one part of forty-six parts of prophethood," and in another narration "forty-three," and in another "seventy." The number in all of these is not intended in itself; what is meant is abundance in the differing degrees, as evidenced by the mention of seventy in some of its transmissions, which for the Arabs signifies abundance. As for what some have held, based on the narration "forty-six," that revelation at its beginning was dreams for six months, which is half a year, while the entire duration of prophethood in Makkah and Madinah was twenty-three years, so half a year is one part of forty-six of it, this is a statement far from precision. For that happened only to the Prophet ﷺ. From where do we know that this period happened to other prophets? Moreover, that only gives the ratio of the time of the dream to the time of prophethood, not the ratio of its reality to the reality of prophethood. When this has become clear to you from what we mentioned first, you know that the meaning of this "part" is the ratio of the first, general readiness shared by mankind to the near, specific readiness belonging to the category of prophets, which is innate to them, may God's blessings be upon them. For that is the distant readiness, though it is general among mankind, and with it are many obstacles and impediments to its actual realization. Among the greatest of these impediments are the outward senses. So God created mankind such that the veil of the senses is lifted through sleep, which is natural to them. The soul, when this veil is lifted, becomes exposed to knowing what it longs for in the world of Truth, and at times it perceives from it a flash in which the attainment of the sought thing occurs. For this reason the Lawgiver made it among the bearers of good tidings, saying: "Nothing remains of prophethood except the bearers of good tidings." They said: "And what are the bearers of good tidings, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The good dream, which a righteous man sees, or which is seen for him."

As for the cause, namely the lifting of the veil of the senses through sleep, it is as I describe to you: The rational soul's perception and actions occur only through the animal spirit (al-ruh al-hayawani), a bodily substance, a subtle vapor whose center is in the left chamber of the heart, according to the anatomical books of Galen and others. It flows with the blood through the arteries and veins, giving sensation, motion, and all bodily actions. Its subtle part rises to the brain, moderating its coldness, and the functions of the faculties in its ventricles are completed. The rational soul perceives and understands only through this vaporous spirit, being attached to it, as the wisdom of creation requires that the subtle does not influence the dense. Since this animal spirit has been refined from among the bodily matters, it became the locus of the effects of the essence distinct from it in its corporeality, which is the rational soul, and its effects came to be present in the body through it.

We have already stated that its perception is of two kinds: perception through the outward, which is by the five senses, and perception through the inward, which is by the cerebral faculties. All this perception diverts it from perceiving what is above it of its spiritual essences, for which it is prepared by nature. Since the outward senses are corporeal, they are subject to languor and weakness, by the fatigue and exhaustion that reaches them, and the spirit is covered by much activity. So God created in it the desire for rest, so that perception may be free in its complete form. This happens only when the animal spirit withdraws from all the outward senses and returns to the inner sense. What aids this is the cold that covers the body at night, so that the innate heat seeks the depths of the body and departs from its surface to its interior. Thus the animal spirit, its vehicle, is carried toward the interior. For this reason, sleep for mankind is mostly at night. When the spirit withdraws from the outward senses, returns to the inner faculties, and the impediments and obstacles of sense lighten for the soul, it returns to the forms that are in the retentive faculty (al-hafizah). From these, through composition and analysis, an imaginal form is represented, most often a familiar one, since it is drawn from perceptions frequently encountered recently. Then the common sense, which is the gatherer of the outward senses, brings it down, and it perceives it in the manner of the five outward senses.

(p-3512) Sometimes the soul turns, in a flash, toward its own spiritual essence, even while it contends with the inner faculties. By its spiritual perception it apprehends, because it is innately disposed to do so, and it draws from the forms of things that have then become attached to its essence. Then the imagination (al-khayal) takes those perceived forms and represents them, either in reality or by imitation, in the familiar moulds. The imitative representations of this kind are those in need of interpretation (ta'bir). Their manipulation by composition and analysis within the forms of the retentive faculty (al-hafizah), before it perceives from that glimpse what it perceives, is "confused dreams" (adghath ahlam).

It is related in the Sahih that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Dreams are of three kinds: a dream from God, a dream from the angel, and a dream from Satan." This division agrees with what we have mentioned: the clear vision is from God, the imitative representation that calls for interpretation is from the angel, and confused dreams are from Satan, since they are all falsehood, and Satan is the fountainhead of falsehood.

This is the reality of the dream, and of what causes and spreads it from sleep. These are properties of the human soul, present in mankind in general; none of them is free of it. Rather, every one of humanity has seen in his sleep what occurred to him in his waking state, many times over, and he has come to a certainty that the soul perceives the unseen during sleep, without doubt. If that is possible in the world of sleep, it is not impossible in other states, because the perceiving essence is one, and its properties are general in every state. End.

He, may God have mercy on him, mentioned, in the discussion of "the science of dream interpretation" (ilm ta'bir al-ru'ya), that the interpretation of dreams existed among the predecessors (al-salaf) just as it does among later generations (al-khalaf), and that Yusuf al-Siddiq, may God's blessings be upon him, used to interpret dreams, as occurs in the Qur'an. Likewise it is established in the Sahih from the Prophet ﷺ and from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. The dream is one of the channels of the unseen, as has preceded. As for the meaning of interpretation, know that the intellectual spirit, when it apprehends its object and casts it to the imagination, which forms it, forms it only in forms suitable to that meaning, in some respect. Among what is seen is that which is explicit and needs no interpretation, owing to its clarity and manifestness, or because of the close resemblance between the perceived and its likeness. For the subject there is a full discussion; consult it there.

(p-3513) And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 7:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask.﴾

﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers﴾, that is, in their story and their account, ﴿are signs﴾, that is, evidences of His power, exalted is He, and His wisdom in everything, ﴿for those who ask﴾, that is, for whoever asks about their news. Or: signs of the prophethood of him (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), for whoever asks about their news, for he informed them of it accurately without having received it from a human being or taken it from a book.

Al-Qashani said: That is, they are majestic signs for whoever asks about their story and knows it, which show them, first: that pure selection (al-istifa', the choosing) is a matter specific to the will of Allah exalted is He, not dependent on the striving of a striver or the desire of one who desires, so they know the ranks of the readinesses (al-isti'dadat) from eternity.

Second: that whomever Allah intends good for, no one can repel it, and whomever Allah protects, no one can direct evil at him or any human being can target him, so their certainty and their reliance upon Him grow strong.

Third: that the scheming of Satan and his seduction is something from which no one is safe, not even the prophets, so they remain on guard against it. And stronger than all of that: it makes them aware, through the path of understanding (al-fahm), which is the mental transition (al-intiqal al-dhihni), of their states at the beginning and the end and what lies between them, and of the manner of their journey to Allah, so it stirs up their longing and their will, sharpens their insight, and strengthens their resolve.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[8] ﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a band. Indeed our father is in manifest error."﴾

﴿When they said, "Joseph and his brother"﴾ — who is Benjamin, his full brother. Their mother was Rachel, daughter of Laban, the maternal uncle of Jacob. ﴿"are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a band"﴾ — i.e., while we are a strong group, more deserving of affection than two young children who offer no support. Al-'usbah and al-'isabah mean a group of men — ten or more — and they were so named because affairs are bound (tu'assab) by them, i.e., strengthened and made firm. Their mention is not merely to convey the number, but to suggest strength, so that the denial becomes more forceful; for they are capable of serving him and striving diligently for his benefit, so how could one who is unable to do that be preferred over them?

﴿"Indeed our father is in manifest error"﴾ — i.e., he has departed from the path of rightness in this matter by preferring, in their opinion, the lesser over the greater. What escaped them was that he loved Joseph because of the signs of excellence he saw in him, especially after that dream; and Benjamin because he was his full brother and the youngest. And it is well known that inclination increases toward the youngest of sons.

And His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 9:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿Kill Joseph or cast him away into some land, so that your father's face will be clear for you, and after him you will be a righteous people.﴾

﴿Kill Joseph or cast him away into some land﴾ is part of their speech related earlier. They said this because the news of the dream had reached them; it is also related that he (Joseph) recounted it to them, so they consulted about plotting against him and said that, and they said: "Let us see afterwards what will come of his dreams," in mockery and derision. The indefiniteness of "land" (arḍan) and its being free of a description is for ambiguity, meaning: in a land unknown, which the father does not know, and it is not possible for Joseph to know the way to reach it.

His saying: ﴿so that your father's face will be clear for you﴾ is the answer to the command, a metaphor for the purity of his love for them, since it indicates his turning to them wholly and his being free from preoccupation with Joseph, so he will occupy himself with them. ﴿And after him you will be﴾ meaning: after finishing with killing him or casting him away, ﴿a righteous people﴾ meaning: repenting to God for what you have committed, so your righteousness will be a ransom for the sin of killing him or casting him away, or your worldly affairs will be set right and your matters will be put in order after him, with your father's face being free (of preoccupation).

(p-3515) Admonitions:

The first: Ibn Ishaq said: "They gathered upon a great matter of severing the ties of kinship, disobedience to a parent, and lack of compassion toward a small child who had committed no sin, and toward an aged, failing elder, the one of right, sanctity and merit, his father; in order to separate him from his son despite his young age, his need for his father's tenderness, and his tranquility in him." May God forgive them.

The second: Ibn Kathir said: "Know that no proof has been established for the prophethood of Joseph's brothers, and the apparent context indicates otherwise. Some people claim that revelation came to them afterwards, but this requires consideration, and whoever claims it needs proof. They have cited nothing except His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 136], and this admits of possibility, because the branches of the Children of Israel are called the Asbat (tribes), just as the Arabs are called qaba'il (tribes) and the non-Arabs shu'ub (peoples). He, exalted is He, mentions that He revealed to prophets from the tribes of the Children of Israel, so He mentioned them collectively because they are many, but each tribe is from the offspring of one man of Joseph's brothers. No proof has been established for the individuals of these that revelation came to them." And God knows best.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[10] ﴿A speaker among them said, "Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well; some of the travelers will pick him up, if you are determined to act."﴾

﴿A speaker among them said﴾ meaning, openly, and the rest agreed to it. ﴿Do not kill Joseph﴾ because killing is among the major sins, which would close the door to reform. He mentioned him by name in place of a pronoun either to arouse their compassion for him or to emphasize the gravity of killing him. ﴿Throw him into the bottom of the well﴾ meaning, into its depths. The (jubb) is a well that has no stones lining it. ﴿Some of the travelers will pick him up﴾ meaning, some of the people who travel (p-3516) through the land, who will take possession of him, so that he cannot return to his father. Thus your aim will be achieved without committing a major sin which would close the door to reform.

﴿If you are determined to act﴾ meaning, resolved and insistent on separating him from his father. It has been narrated that the speaker was their eldest brother, the firstborn of Ya'qub (Ruben).

When they agreed upon his opinion:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 11:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[11] ﴿They said, "O our father, what is [wrong] with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph while we are indeed sincere toward him?"﴾

﴿They said﴾, i.e., to their father, ﴿"O our father, what is [wrong] with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph while we are indeed sincere toward him?"﴾ That is: why do you fear for him at our hands, when we wish him good, love him, and are compassionate toward him? By this they intended to draw him away from his habit of protecting him from them. And in it is evidence that he sensed from them something that made him unwilling to entrust him to them — thus stated in al-Kashshaf.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 12:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿Send him with us tomorrow, to frolic and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.﴾

﴿Send him with us tomorrow, to frolic and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.﴾ Al-ratʿ (ar-rat') means eating, drinking, moving about and being active, wherever there is greenery, water and crops. They mean: your requiring him to remain in your presence necessarily causes him weariness, which cuts off his vigor for worship and for acquiring perfections.

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[13] ﴿He said: "It grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾

﴿He said: "It grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ (p-3517) That is: even if you claim that you will be his guardians, your guarding of him only exists so long as you are watching him, but a person is not free from heedlessness, so I fear your heedlessness concerning him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He excused himself to them for two things:

The first: that their taking him away and their separation from him grieves him, for he could not bear to be without him even for an hour.

The second: his fear for him from the attack of the wolf if they became heedless of him, through their pasturing and playing, or if their concern for him lessened, and their care for guarding him was not sincere.

Al-Nasir said: The more pressing of the two matters on his heart was the fear of the wolf for him, because it is the likely cause of his destruction. As for his grief at parting from him for a while, during which he would graze, play, and return safe to him shortly, that is a light matter. So it was as though they did not concern themselves except with reassuring him and calming him about the more severe of the two matters for him. End of quote. That is, in what was related of them by His saying:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[14] ﴿They said: "If the wolf eats him while we are a band, then we would indeed be losers."﴾

﴿They said: "If the wolf eats him while we are a band"﴾ i.e., a group of strong men, able to snatch him from the wolf's jaws. ﴿then we would indeed be losers﴾ i.e., destroyed through weakness and cowardice. Or incapable, or deserving to be cursed with ruin and perdition.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[15] ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well. And We revealed to him, "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive."﴾

﴿So when they took him away﴾, meaning after they had argued with their father about him. ﴿And agreed to put him into the depths of the well﴾. In this there is an emphasis on the magnitude of what they resolved upon, since they took him as though to honour him, to bring joy to their father, and yet they plotted what they plotted. ﴿And We revealed to him, "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs"﴾, meaning We made him know by casting it into his heart, or through an angel at that moment, as good news to him that you will be delivered from what you are in and will tell them what they did to you.

His saying ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ may be connected to "revealed", meaning We revealed that to him while they did not perceive, as a comfort to him and a removal of loneliness. Or it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the hāʾ in "lataṇabbi'annahum", meaning: that you will inform them of that while they do not perceive that you are Joseph, because of the loftiness of your station, as will come in His saying: ﴿So he recognized them, but they did not recognize him﴾ [Yusuf: 58].

It was narrated that they stripped Joseph of his embroidered shirt that he was wearing, took him, and cast him into the well, and it was empty, with no water in it. Then they sat down, eating and amusing themselves until evening.

The answer to "lammā" (when) in the verse is omitted, like "they did what they did", or "they cast him into it". It was also said that the answer is "wa-awḥaynā" (and We revealed), with the wāw being superfluous.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[16] ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.﴾

"And they came to their father in the evening, weeping" explains their deception of their father by way of an apology that gives the impression of his death, the decisive cutting-off of what he hopes for, so that his love for him would be severed, even if after a while, and he would then return to them with complete love. They came in the evening because it is the time of darkness, which prevents him from examining them closely in the false excuse and from scrutinizing their faces for the lie. By their weeping and their outward show of grief over him, they gave the impression of the extent of their love for him, which prevents them from daring to do him harm. Then they called him by the title "father," attributed to them, so that he would have mercy on them and set aside his anger toward them, which would otherwise prompt him to disbelieve them.

**The commentary on His words, Exalted is He:**

[17] ﴿They said, "O our father, we went off racing one another and left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾

﴿They said, "O our father, we went off racing one another"﴾, meaning in running and in shooting arrows. ﴿and left Joseph by our belongings﴾, meaning the goods they enjoyed, including clothing, provisions and other things, so that he would guard them. ﴿and the wolf devoured him﴾, meaning just as you feared.

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful﴾, this is a great display of tact in establishing what they were attempting. They are saying: "We know that you will not believe us in this situation, even if we were truthful with you, so how much less when you accuse us and have no confidence in what we say?!"

Several rulings have been derived from the verse:

Among them: a person's weeping does not prove his truthfulness, since it may be feigned. This was related by Ibn al-'Arabi.

Among them: the permissibility of racing. It includes, in terms of medicine (ṭibb), the training of the soul and of animals and the exercising of the limbs for skilled handling. This is stated in *al-Iklil*.

Some Yemenis said: Play among children is permissible so long as it contains no harm and does not imitate the wicked. As for play among adults, it has three categories:

The first: that it has the nature of gambling (qimar), in which case it is not permitted.

The second: that it does not have that nature, and it involves aid and encouragement toward strength and jihad, such as archery contests and horse races. Such play is permitted by consensus.

The third: that it involves no stake, such as wrestling and the like. On this the Shafi'is have two opinions, and the permissibility is preferred if there is no stake, or if the stake is given willingly. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) wrestled Yazid ibn Rukanah.

It is related that Aisha said: "I raced the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) twice. I outran him the first time, but when I had gained weight he outran me and said: 'This is for that.'"

And in a hadith: "Three kinds of play are not part of frivolity: a man's playing with his wife, his training of his horse, and his shooting with his bow." End.

(p-3520) The Interpretation (ta'wil) of His Words, Exalted is He:

[18] ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood.[?] He said, "Rather, your souls have embellished a matter for you. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾

﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾ is an explanation of the scheme they had plotted. They took his striped shirt and dipped it in the blood of a goat they had slaughtered. "False" (kadhib) is a verbal noun (masdar) with an implied modifier, meaning "possessing falsehood." Or it is described by it for emphasis, as in "a man of justice" (rajul 'adl). "Upon" ('ala) is an adverbial complement of "they came" (ja'u), which implies the meaning of "they fabricated" (iftarau).

His words, ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have embellished a matter for you"﴾, mean: regarding Joseph's disappearance, his separation from me, and the false excuse.

Al-Nasir said: "What strengthened his suspicion of them is that they claimed a specific circumstance that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, had feared would lead to his destruction, namely the wolf eating him. So he suspected they had seized upon the excuse from his words to them: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him﴾ [Yusuf: 13]. False excuses often coincide with the anxiety of the one who is being addressed in the excuse, to the point that some commanders of the believers would instruct a thief to deny the theft." End of quotation.

In al-Iklil, it is inferred from this the ruling based on indicators (al-hukm bil-amarat) and the consideration of suspicion (al-nazar ila al-tuhma), in that he said: ﴿Rather, your souls have embellished...﴾, the verse.

Subtleties (lata'if):

Al-Mahayimi said: Among the benefits of the verse is that status (jah) calls to envy, as wealth does, and it prevents genuine love that arises from kinship and the like. Rather, it makes their enmity fiercer than the enmity of strangers. Envy calls to plotting against the one envied and against whoever cares for him. It arises only when the schemer sees himself as more perfect in intellect than the one he schemes against. Whoever claims advice, protection and love, and even displays them in action, is not to be relied upon by one who is envious. Likewise, whoever displays trustworthiness in word and deed may commit betrayal. Humiliation and honor are in the hand of Allah, not of creation. Whoever seeks his aim through disobeying Allah is distanced from it. Fear of creation brings about trial. Even if a human is a prophet, he is first created with the nature of humanity. Following desires brings about long sorrow. Destiny is certain, and caution does not avert destiny.

It was said to the hoopoe: "How do you see water beneath the earth, yet you do not see the net above it?" He said: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind."

Tasweel (embellishment) is the adorning of the self for a person of what he desires, and the depiction of the ugly in the form of the beautiful. ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾: "patience" (sabr) is either a predicate or a subject, since it is qualified, meaning "my condition is beautiful patience." Or it means "so patience is more beautiful." Patience is the strength of the soul to bear pains such as calamities when they befall. The beautiful kind of it is that in which there is no complaint to creation and no impatience, being content with Allah's decree and standing by what servitude requires.

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾: meaning, He is the one from whom help is sought to bear what you describe of Joseph's destruction (so they had estimated it). Abu al-Su'ud verified that the meaning is to reveal the state of what you describe and to show that it is a lie and to show Joseph's safety, since it is a sign of falsehood. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat: 180]. This is most fitting with what comes later, His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So patience is beautiful. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ [Yusuf: 83]. Interpreting "the One sought for help" as bearing what they describe of Joseph's destruction and patience over the calamity regarding him is rejected by his, peace be upon him, denial of their claim in that matter, and the form of the expression does not support it, since it is predominantly used for describing something with what is not in it, as has been indicated. End of quotation.

In His words, ﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought﴾, there is an acknowledgment that his being endowed with patience does not occur except through His assistance.

Al-Razi said: Because the psychological motives call him to show distress, and they are strong. The spiritual motives call him to patience and contentment. It is as if the two are in conflict and struggle. So if Allah's assistance is not obtained, victory is not achieved. His words, ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, correspond to His words, ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5], and His words, ﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought﴾, correspond to His words, ﴿And You alone we seek help from﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. End of quotation.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned what befell Joseph in the well, after what had preceded with His words:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[19] ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, so he lowered his bucket. He said: "Good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise. But Allah knows what they do.﴾

﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer﴾, meaning the one who comes to the water and draws it for them. ﴿so he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning he sent it down into the well to fill it, and Yusuf took hold of it to come out. When he saw him, ﴿he said: "Good news! This is a boy!"﴾. It is also read as (يا بُشْرايَ, "O my good news"), with the genitive construction, and the vocative particle is then omitted. Or he is placed in the position of one who calls out. It is said that this word is used for giving glad tidings without intending a real address.

Al-Zajjaj said: The sense of the address in these matters, which do not answer, is to alert the listeners and to emphasize the story. When you say "Oh, how strange!" (يا عَجَباهُ), it is as if you said: "Be amazed!"

And (al-ghulam, "the boy") means one who has just begun to grow a beard, or one from his birth until he reaches youth. The tanwin (nunation) on it is for magnification.

﴿And they hid him as merchandise﴾, meaning they concealed him as goods for trade. So ﴿بِضاعَةً (bidaʿatan, "as merchandise")﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). In al-Fara'id it is stated that he included in (أسَرُّوهُ, "they hid him") the meaning of (جَعَلُوهُ, "they made him"), i.e., they made him merchandise while concealing it, so it is a direct object, or an object of purpose, meaning: for the sake of trade. And (al-biḍaʿah, "merchandise") is from al-bidʿ, which means cutting, because it is a substantial piece of wealth kept for trade. ﴿But Allah knows what they do﴾.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 20:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[20] ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, and they were of those who were indifferent to him.﴾

﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, and they were of those who were indifferent to him.﴾ The pronoun in (asarrūhu, "they concealed him") and (sharawhu, "they sold him") refers to the caravan (al-sayyarah), because it carries the sense of a company of travelers. It has been related that they were merchants from the town of Madyan. When their water-drawer (wārid) had drawn up Yusuf and they had taken him into their merchandise, they sold him to a caravan passing by them on its way to Egypt for twenty dirhams of silver; then they brought Yusuf to Egypt. The word (darāhima, "dirhams") is an apposition (badal) to (thaman, "price"). The word (al-ma'dūd, "counted") is a metaphor (kināyah) for scarcity, because large amounts were weighed by them. The word (al-zuhd, "indifference") in it means aversion to it.

Benefits:

In (al-Iklil) it is said: People have derived from this verse the rulings concerning the foundling (luqayt). From it they took that the foundling is to be taken up and not left behind. From His saying, (this is a boy, ghulam), [it is derived] that he was young, and that picking up (iltiqat) is specific to such a one, so an adult is not picked up. Likewise His saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], because that is a matter specific to children. From His saying: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾ [it is derived] that the foundling is judged to be free, and that the price of a free person is unlawful. Some of them said: The basis of the inference is that they sold him for a base price because he was a foundling, and he cannot be owned; for if he could be owned, they would have collected his full price.

Some of the Zaydis said, and this inference was refuted on the grounds that their action is not a law (shari'ah). As for now, there is no doubt that the apparent status of the foundling is freedom, just as his apparent status is Islam. End of quotation.

Al-Mahayimi said: Among the benefits is that relief may come from where one does not expect it, and that one should await relief in hardship. And that one who goes out seeking something may find what was not in his mind. And that a grave matter may present in it what makes it easier. And that good news may be followed by sorrow, and honor may be followed by humiliation, and vice versa. End of quotation.

(p-٣٥٢٤) Discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[21] ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence honorable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." And thus did We establish Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant in His affair, but most of the people do not know.﴾

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence honorable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son."﴾ He, exalted is He, informs of His gentleness toward Joseph, for He facilitated for him the one who bought him in Egypt, so he took care of him, instructed his household, and perceived in him goodness and righteousness. The meaning of ﴿Make his residence honorable﴾ is: make his station good and pleasing. Al-mathwa (the residence) is the place of lodging (ath-thawa'), which is dwelling.

Al-Shihab said: Honoring his residence is a metonymy for honoring him in the most eloquent and complete manner, because whoever honors the place where a guest stays, by providing good beds, spreads, and the like, has honored his guest with all that he may be honored with. Or "al-mathwa" is an inserted (redundant) word, as one says: "al-maqam as-sami" (the lofty station).

It is narrated that when the caravan arrived in Egypt, the chief of the police (ra'is ash-shurta) at the court of the King of Egypt bought him from them, and he stayed in his master's house, while divine care enveloped him and success surrounded him. His master saw that whatever he undertook, Allah, exalted is He, made successful at his hand, so he gained favor in his sight and appointed him overseer over all that he possessed, and Allah, exalted is He, multiplied the blessing in his crops, his wealth, and his property.

﴿And thus did We establish Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events﴾ That is: just as We granted him a noble residence in the house of the Aziz and in his heart, We granted him authority to command and forbid, and an elevated standing in the land of Egypt, and prestige among its people, and love in their hearts, so that the outcome of that would be his being taught the interpretation of the dream that the king would see, and that would lead Joseph to supreme leadership.

﴿And Allah is predominant in His affair﴾ That is: He cannot be prevented from what He wills, nor is He contested in what He intends. Or (it means) over the affair of Joseph, for what was intended for him of trial was intended more than once, yet nothing happened except what Allah willed for him of the praiseworthy outcome.

(p-٣٥٢٥) ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ That is: the entire matter is in His hand, so they come and go claiming that they have some share of the affair. Or they do not know the subtleties of His workmanship and the hidden aspects of His kindness.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 22:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ This verse is like the one before it: it is interwoven within the fabric of the narrative for a wonderful purpose, namely to hasten the announcement of the outcomes of Joseph's patience, the fruits of his striving, and the marvels of God's exalted handiwork in fulfilling His purposes, for He stored up for him bounties within those trials and reserved for him sovereignty within that servitude. The meaning of ﴿reached his maturity﴾ is the time when his body and strength had fully developed.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say, "So-and-so reached his maturity (ashuddahu)," when he has attained the peak of his youth and strength before beginning to decline. As for ﴿al-hukm﴾ (judgment), it may mean ḥikmah (wisdom), which is knowledge supported by action, or it may mean judgment among people.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾, there is an indication that he was a good-doer in his conduct, mindful of God at the outset of his affair, and that God gave him judgment and knowledge as a reward for his goodness.

And it is reported from al-Hasan: Whoever worships his Lord well in his youth, God will give him wisdom in his old age.

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[23] ﴿The woman in whose house he was sought to seduce him from himself. She bolted the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence comfortable. Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed."﴾

This returns to explaining what happened to Joseph in the house of the Governor (al-'Aziz) after he had ordered his wife to honour Joseph's lodging: her solicitation of him and his refusal.

*Al-muraawada* (solicitation, i.e. pressing someone to do something) means demanding. That is, she asked him to have intercourse with her. Its construction with *'an* (from) is because it implies the sense of deceiving. The text avoids naming her in order to preserve secrecy and concealment, and uses the relative pronoun without naming the Governor's wife, to establish the solicitation, since his being in her house is itself something that invites it. It was said to a woman: "What led you to do what has no good in it?" She said: "The nearness of the cushion and the length of the night." The verse also serves to show the full purity of Joseph, peace be upon him, as will come later.

*Haita* (هَيْتَ) is read like *layta*, *qila* and *haythu*, and with a kasra on the *ha'*, with a silent hamza after it, and with the *ta'* either fatha or damma. In all these dialects it is an *ism fi'l* (a verb-noun, a word functioning as an imperative verb) meaning "come". The *lam* is to specify the object, i.e. the addressee. It is reported from al-Farra' that it is a dialect of the people of Hawran that spread to Mecca, and they spoke with it.

Ibn al-Abyari said: This is an agreement between the dialect of Quraysh and the people of Hawran, just as the Arabs and the Romans agreed on *al-qistas* (balance) and similar words.

*Ma'adha Allah* (معاذَ اللَّهِ) is in the accusative as a *masdar* (verbal noun in the accusative of the absolute object). That is: I seek refuge in God with a seeking, from what you are calling me to, because it is adultery and betrayal of what I have been entrusted with, and harm to one who expects benefit, and wrongdoing towards one who has been good.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is his avoidance in the most complete manner, and an indication of the reasoning that it is a monstrous evil, from which one must seek refuge in God Most High for deliverance. That is only because he, peace be upon him, had witnessed by the clear proof that God Most High had shown him what it is in itself of utmost ugliness and extreme wickedness.

His words, ﴿Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence comfortable﴾, are a justification for refusing on the basis of some external causes, which might have an effect on her and encourage her to take them into account, after drawing attention to his own intrinsic reason, which she would almost accept, given what her own soul had embellished for her. The pronoun refers to the matter in question (*al-sha'n*, the pronoun of the situation). The benefit of beginning the sentence with it is to announce the greatness of its content, together with the fact that it reinforces it in the mind. For the pronoun, at first, conveys only an undefined matter of importance, so the mind remains waiting for what follows, and when it arrives it takes firm hold. It is as if it were said: this momentous matter, namely, "my lord", that is, my master the Governor, "has made my residence comfortable", that is, has taken care of me, since he ordered you to honour me; so how can I possibly wrong him by betraying him in his household? In this there is guidance for her to observe the right of the Governor in the most gracious way.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, and "my lord" is the predicate, with *inna* and "has made my residence comfortable" as a second predicate. Or, it is the predicate, and the first (word) is an apposition to the pronoun. The meaning is: the situation is thus; how then could I disobey Him by committing that great indecency? In this there is a warning to her about the punishment of God, Mighty and Majestic. In both interpretations, limiting the statement to mentioning this condition without addressing the refusal of what she invited him to do is an indication that this level of clarification is sufficient to show that it is impossible for him, and that it is something that does not fall under the possibility of occurrence at all.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed﴾, are a justification for the refusal mentioned, following one justification after another. *Al-falah* (success) is victory, or remaining in goodness. The meaning of *aflaha* is that one entered into it, like *asbaha* and its sisters (verbs of becoming). By "the wrongdoers" is meant everyone who does wrong, whoever he may be, so that in this are included, in the first instance, those who repay goodness with evil, and those who disobey the command of God Most High. It was said: it means fornicators, because they wrong themselves, and wrong the one whose household they violate. End.

One of the Yemeni scholars said: The fruits of this verse are three:

The first: that when one is called to disobedience, it is obligatory to seek refuge in God from that, so that He may protect him from it. This includes the call of Satan, the call of human devils, and the call of the desire of the soul.

The second: that the master and the owner is called *rabb* (lord).

The third: that it is permissible to abandon the ugly because it is ugly, and to observe the right of another, and to fear shame, or poverty, or fear, and the like. It should not be said that the association (of these reasons with abandoning evil) is not beneficial in his being one who abandons evil, and that he is not rewarded for it. It also indicates the necessity of the goodness of reciprocating kindness with kindness, and that whoever fails to reciprocate it is a wrongdoer. End.

(p-3528) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[24] ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾

﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾

Al-hamm (concern, desire): it can mean intention and will. It can also be stronger than mere will but weaker than resolve (al-'azm). When it means the soul gathering itself toward a matter and determining upon it, and al-'azm means the intention to carry it out, then hamm is the first stage of resolve. This is the meaning of the saying of the scholars: "Hamm is of two kinds: a hamm that remains with it resolve, commitment and approval, which is blameworthy and for which one is held accountable; and a hamm in the sense of a passing thought and inner talk, without determination, for which one is not held accountable. For the occurrence of forbidden things in the breasts and their being imagined in the minds does not incur accountability as long as they have not come into being in external reality."

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and the authors of the Sunan transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, as long as they do not speak it or act upon it." It was also narrated by al-Tabarani from 'Imran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both.

So the meaning of His saying, ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, is: she desired intimacy with him, meaning she intended it and resolved upon it with a firm resolve that no deterrent could turn her from, after she had already engaged in its beginnings: enticing him, bolting the doors, and calling him to hasten to her with her words, ﴿Come, you!﴾ [Yusuf: 23], which compelled him to flee toward the door.

As for His saying, ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾: that is, had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her as she desired him, because the incentives were abundant. But he saw, through Allah's support of him with proof, what turned him away from evil and immorality.

(p-3529) Abu Hayyan said: "A parallel to this is (you committed sin, had Allah not preserved you)." We do not say that the answer of lawla (لَوْلا) precedes it, even though there is no proof for its prohibition. Rather, the explicit conditional particles that govern are a matter of disagreement, to the extent that the Kufans and the leading Basrans held that it may precede. Rather, we say: it is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. For the omitted element in a conditional is estimated to be of the same kind as what precedes it." End of quote.

Thus the verse, in that case, clearly states that he did not desire at all. It has also been said that the answer of lawla is "it would have covered her" or the like. In that case, the meaning of hamm is what Imam al-Razi said: that it is the passing of a thing into the mind, or the inclination of nature, like the fasting person in summer who sees cold water, and his soul inclines him toward it and to drinking it, but his religion prevents him from it. And like a woman of surpassing beauty and loveliness who presents herself to a young man in the prime of his strength, so that between desire and chastity, and between the soul and the intellect, there is a pulling and a struggle. Here, hamm is an expression for the pulls of natural disposition, while seeing the proof is the pull of wisdom. This does not indicate that a sin occurred. Rather, the stronger this state is, the more complete is the strength to fulfill the requirements of servitude." End of quote.

Likewise Abu al-Su'ud said: "His desire for her means his inclination toward her, according to the demands of human nature and the desire and ardor of youth, an innate inclination which hardly falls under legal obligation, and not that he intended her by deliberate choice. Do you not see what preceded of his steadfast refusal, which indicates his complete aversion to it and his revulsion from it, and his judgment that the wrongdoers will not prosper? Is this not, rather, a firm record of the impossibility of desire proceeding from him, peace be upon him? He expressed it as hamm only for the sake of its occurring in the company of her hamm in the mention, by way of figurative correspondence (al-mushakala), not because of any resemblance to it, as has been said. Their difference has been pointed out, in that the two were not joined in one phrase of expression, such as saying: 'And they both certainly desired intimacy,' or 'each of them desired the other.' The first was introduced with what establishes its existence through emphatic oath, and the second was followed by what removes its effect, in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, that is, His overwhelming argument, indicating the complete ugliness of fornication and the evil of its path. The meaning of his seeing it is the completeness of his certainty, and his witnessing of it was a witnessing reaching the level of the certainty of sight. It is as though he, peace be upon him, had witnessed fornication (p-3530) through that clear proof, in its own essence as the most ugly thing and that which most requires one to beware of it. For this reason he did what he did of steadfast refusal, and the judgment that whoever commits it will not prosper." End of quote.

The answer of lawla is omitted, and the context indicates it. That is: had it not been for witnessing the proof of his Lord regarding fornication, he would have followed the demand of his innate inclination. But since he had witnessed it before, he continued in what the proof required of him. The benefit of this conditional statement is to show that his, peace be upon him, abstention was not due to the absence of support from natural inclination, but to pure chastity and purity, despite the abundance of inner incentives and the arrangement of external circumstances that would make the natural judgments manifest." End of quote.

It is therefore clear that there is no doubt in it concerning the infallibility ('isma) of Yusuf, peace be upon him. For prophets are not immune from inner talk and the passing impulses of innate desire, but they are immune from obeying them and yielding to them. Had there been no innate incentives in them, they would have been either angels or a different kind of being, and they would not have been rewarded for abstaining from forbidden things, because they would have been compelled to abstain by nature. The impotent man is not rewarded or recompensed for abstaining from fornication, because reward is only for an act, and abstention without an incentive is not an act. But abstention with an incentive is the restraint of the soul from what it longs for, and that is an inner act.

The true meaning of the infallibility of the prophets is their purity and their distance from committing indecencies and abominations, for which they were sent to purify people; so that they would not become a bad example, corrupting morals and manners, and a proof for the foolish to violate the sanctities of the laws. Its meaning is not that they are gods, exempt from everything human nature requires.

Now, some commentators who are fond of narrating reports have attached here what they picked up from the People of the Book and from the pious-seeming, of those fabricated tales about Yusuf, peace be upon him, concerning his desire, which I hold my work too pure to transmit, rejecting them. All of them, as al-'Allama Abu al-Su'ud said, are fables and falsehoods which ears reject and minds and intellects refuse. Woe to whoever recites and fabricates them, or hears them and believes them. Al-Zamakhshari preceded him and excelled in refuting them, so let it be examined, for it is something that pleases the one who reads it.

As for (al-su') (السُّوءُ): the reprehensible, lewdness, and the disliked. And (al-fahsha') (الفَحْشاءُ): that whose ugliness has reached its extreme.

Abu al-Su'ud said: "In His saying, ﴿that We might avert from him﴾, etc., there is a clear sign and a conclusive proof that he, peace and blessings be upon him, never had any desire for disobedience, nor did he ever turn toward it. Otherwise it would have said: 'that We might avert him from evil and immorality.' Rather, that impulse was directed at him from outside, and Allah the Exalted averted it by what He placed in him of the requirements of chastity and infallibility. So reflect."

(Al-mukhlisin) (المُخْلِصِينَ) was recited with a kasra on the lam, meaning those who have made their religion sincere for Allah, and with a fatha, meaning those whom Allah has made sincere for His obedience, by preserving them.

Al-Shihab said: "It has been said that everyone who had any involvement in this story testified to his innocence, peace be upon him. Allah the Exalted testified by His saying, ﴿that We might avert﴾, etc. He testified himself by his saying, ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me﴾ [Yusuf: 26], and similar. The wife of the nobleman testified by her saying, ﴿And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he refused﴾ [Yusuf: 32], and her master by his saying, ﴿Indeed, you were among the sinners﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. And Iblis by his saying, ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 83], so his statement included the fact that he did not mislead him. And despite all this, the storytellers did not exonerate him." End of quote. May Allah pardon them.

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[25] ﴿And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they met her husband at the door. She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your wife except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾

﴿And they both raced to the door﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, were it not that he had seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf: 24], etc., and His saying: ﴿Thus [it was]﴾ [Yusuf: 24], etc. It is an acknowledgment placed between the two conjoined clauses to affirm his innocence. The meaning is: She certainly desired him, and he refused, and they both raced to the door, meaning each sought to get ahead of the other to the door: Yusuf, peace be upon him, to leave, and she to prevent him from leaving. He made the word "the door" singular here though he had used the plural earlier, because what is meant by "the door" is the outer door, through which lies the escape.

(p-3532) ﴿And she tore his shirt from behind﴾ meaning she pulled him from behind so that it was torn, i.e., his shirt was split.

﴿And they met her husband at the door﴾ meaning they came upon her husband there, arriving.

﴿She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your wife except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾ — to clear her own character and to incite [the husband] against him.

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil, the reasoned explanation of a text's meaning) of His saying, exalted is He:

[26] ﴿He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me," and a witness from her family testified, "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars."﴾

﴿He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me," and a witness from her family testified, "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars."﴾ Because tearing it from the front is a sign that she was defending herself with it, or that he stumbled over the front parts of his shirt because he was approaching her, so it was torn as he hurried after her.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[27] ﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.﴾

﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.﴾ Because it is a sign of his turning away from her, owing to the fact that she followed him, pulled his garment toward herself, and tore it.

Among the subtleties (lata'if) is what has been said: this witness wanted not to be the one who exposed her, and he was confident that the tearing of his shirt was only from behind. So setting it up as a sign of his truthfulness and her lying, he then mentioned the other case, that it was torn from the front, knowing that it had not been torn from the front until he had cleared himself of the accusation in testimony and of intent to disgrace, and so that he would be fair to both of them. He mentions a sign of her truthfulness, whose negation is known, just as he mentioned a sign of his truthfulness, whose existence is known. For this reason he placed the sign of her truthfulness before the sign of his truthfulness in the mention, to remove the accusation, and out of confidence that the second sign is the one that actually occurs, so its delay does no harm. This very subtlety, and God knows best, (p-3533) is what the believing man of Pharaoh's family observed in his saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, upon him is his lie, and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. He placed the case of lying before the case of truthfulness, to remove the accusation he feared might reach Musa, peace be upon him, and out of confidence that the second case, which is his truthfulness, is the one that actually occurs, so its delay in mention does no harm for this benefit. For this reason he said: ﴿some of what he promises you﴾ [Ghafir: 28], and did not say "all that he promises you," hinting that they were in league with him against him, and that he was eager to deprive him of his right. A similar approach is the delaying by Yusuf, peace be upon him, of the uncovering of his brother's bag, which is mentioned later, because had he begun with it they would have realized that he was the one who ordered the cup to be placed in it, and God knows best.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[28] ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed, it is from your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾

﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed, it is from your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ By "guile" (kayd) is meant cunning (hilah) and deceit (makr). He magnified their guile because it is subtler, more adhering to the heart, and more forceful in its effect upon the soul; in it there is finesse (niqah) and gentleness (rifq), and by it women overcome men.

Admonition (tanbih):

Ibn al-Furs said: Whoever holds that judgment may be made by indications and signs where clear proofs are not present cites this verse, as in the case of found property (luqatah), theft, deposits (wadi'ah), the marks of walls (ma'aqid al-hitan), ceilings and the like.

And the Most High's words:

The discussion of the words of His, exalted is He: [ 29 ] "Joseph, turn away from this, and ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of those who erred."

"Joseph, turn away from this" — he is addressed with the particle of address omitted, due to his nearness and his complete attentiveness to the matter under discussion.

That is: "O Joseph, turn away from this affair, conceal it, and do not speak of it."

"And ask forgiveness for your sin" — that is, for what came from you of intending evil toward this young man, and then slandering him with what he is innocent of.

"Indeed, you were of those who erred" — that is, among the company of those who deliberately commit sin. It is said: khati'a (خَطِئَ) when one sins deliberately, and akhta'a (أخْطَأ) when one does it without intention. For this reason one says: asaba al-khata' (أصابَ الخَطَأ), akhta'a al-sawab (أخْطَأ الصَّوابَ), and asaba al-sawab (أصابَ الصَّوابَ).
