On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:

[47] ﴿He said: "You will sow for seven years in succession. Whatever you harvest, leave it in its ears, except for a little of which you eat."﴾

[48] ﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except for a little of what you have kept aside.﴾ [Yusuf: 48]

[49] ﴿Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain, and in which they will press (juice).﴾ [Yusuf: 49]

﴿He said﴾, that is, Yusuf, in interpreting it: ﴿You will sow for seven years in succession﴾, that is, persistently and diligently, every year of them. ﴿Whatever you harvest﴾, that is, of the crop. ﴿Leave it in its ears﴾, that is, do not thresh it, for this keeps it better. ﴿Except for a little of which you eat﴾, that is, during those years, meaning in the amount you eat.

﴿Then after that﴾ [Yusuf: 48], that is, after the aforementioned seven years, ﴿will come seven hard years﴾ [Yusuf: 48], that is, seven years difficult for the people because of the severity of the famine. ﴿Which will consume what you have stored up for them﴾ [Yusuf: 48], that is, the grains you have set aside for them, left in their ears. Since he expressed the cows by "years," he attributed the eating to the years, just as he saw in the vision the cows eating, so that there is correspondence between the thing expressed, which is what was seen in the dream, and the thing by which it is expressed, which is its interpretation. The rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli, a figurative attribution of an action to something other than its true agent), meaning "it is eaten in them," is not required, as in the phrase "his day is fasting," because it may be a case of mushakala (a figure of speech in which a word is used because of its association with another word in the same context) in that context. ﴿Except for a little of what you keep aside﴾ [Yusuf: 48], that is, what you guard and store up for sowing.

﴿Then after that﴾ [Yusuf: 48], that is, after the years described as hard, and the consumption of the stored grain, ﴿will come a year in which the people will be given rain﴾ [Yusuf: 49], that is, they will receive rain, or they will be relieved from the drought, or He will lift from them what they dislike through relief. ﴿And in which they will press (juice)﴾ [Yusuf: 49], that is, what they used to press according to their custom, such as grapes, olives, and the like.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The mention of "pressing" (al-'asr), although it could have been dispensed with by mentioning "rain," which normally entails it, just as he dispensed with mentioning their handling of the grains, is either because rain does not entail pressing in the same way that it entails grains, since the things mentioned depend for their good condition on other causes besides rain; or it is out of consideration for the one asking, taking into account his particular situation, as good news for him. This is the point on which the excellence of the placement of his (Yusuf's) inclusion among "the people" depends, in the reading with the second-person ta' (the reading in which the verb is addressed to the people, with the letter ta' placed above). It has been said that the meaning of "they press" is "they milk the udders." End of quote.

The wording, in its general meaning, includes this, because milking involves squeezing the udder so that the milk comes out.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The interpretation of the fat cows and the green ears is fertile years, and of the lean and dry ones is barren years. Then, after finishing the interpretation of the dream, he gave them the good news that the eighth year would come blessed, fertile, abundant in goodness and plentiful in blessings, and that this came by way of revelation.

**Note:**

Al-Iklil (The Crown) said: This verse is among the foundations of dream interpretation. It also shows that the dreams of unbelievers can be valid, that it is permissible to call him (the king) a "king," and that our saying "dreams belong to the first interpreter" is not a general rule for every dream. This is because they said: ﴿confused dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 44], and their saying this did not make the dream void. Thus the rule applies only to a dream that admits several possible meanings, one of which is interpreted and then comes to pass. In His words ﴿Then after that will come a year﴾ [Yusuf: 49], etc., there is an addition beyond what was asked about, from which it is inferred that there is no harm in doing this in both dream interpretation and giving religious rulings (fatwa). End of quote.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 50:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[50] ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what is the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me."﴾ That is, bring him out of the prison and present him, because of what he knew of his knowledge and virtue. ﴿When the messenger came to him﴾ — that is, to summon him to the king — ﴿he said﴾ — that is, Yusuf said to him: ﴿Return to your lord﴾ — that is, to your master, the king — ﴿and ask him what is the case of the women who cut their hands﴾ — that is, what is their affair and their story? He commanded him to ask and inquire about that, and he did not reveal the story to him nor explain it to him; for a general question stirs the king to uncover, investigate and seek information, so that innocence is achieved. A general question stirs a person and moves him to search into it, because he is averse to one who is ignorant of it and lacks knowledge of it. Had he said, "Ask him to examine that matter," it would have been a request for investigation into it, which one tolerates and treats lightly, and it would have been a boldness toward him, so he might refuse it and not heed it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He only delayed and deliberated in answering the king, and he put forward the question of the women, in order to show the innocence of his good name from what he was accused of and imprisoned for, lest the envious climb up by means of it to disparage his affair before him, and make it a ladder to lowering his standing with him, and lest they say: "He only remained in prison for a grave matter and a great crime, which deserves that he be imprisoned and tormented and his evil restrained." In this is evidence that striving to dispel accusations is obligatory, the obligation of avoiding standing in their places. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him not stand in places of accusation." (p-3551) From this: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to those passing by him while he was in seclusion, and with him was one of his wives: "She is so-and-so," in order to avert suspicion.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have marvelled at Yusuf, at his generosity and his patience, and God forgives him, when he was asked about the lean and fat cows. Had I been in his place, I would not have informed them until I stipulated that they bring me out. And I have marvelled at him when the messenger came to him and he said: ﴿Return to your lord﴾. Had I been in his place and remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have hastened to respond and rushed to the door, and I would not have sought an excuse, if he was indeed forbearing, possessed of deliberation." End.

Abd al-Razzaq related it in his Musannaf as a mursal narration from Ikrimah.

It has also been related in the Musnad and the two Sahihs, in abridged form, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Had I remained in prison as long as Yusuf remained, I would have answered the caller." The Prophet (ﷺ) praised him for this deliberation, and within this praise for patience and steadfastness is his exoneration and vindication from what might come to the mind as a suspicion, that he had intended a desire toward the wife of the Aziz for which he would be blamed; for if he endured and remained steadfast in what he was not required to endure, namely leaving the prison, while the motives to leave it were abundant, then to endure in what was incumbent upon him to endure of desire is more fitting and more worthy. Thus reported al-Nasir.

Abu al-Su'ud said: He did not mention the wife of the Aziz, despite what he suffered from her of the sorrows, out of safeguarding the obligations of rights, and guarding against her plotting, since he considered her to remain on the brink of enmity. As for the women, he had hoped to make them speak the truth, and that they would testify to her confession that she had solicited him, and he refused. For this reason he restricted himself to describing them with the cutting of hands, and did not explicitly mention their solicitation of him or their saying "Obey your mistress," and he sufficed with alluding to that by his saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot﴾, meaning what they plotted against him. In attributing His knowledge to God is an indication of its greatness, and that its essence is not hoped to be reached, but what cannot be wholly grasped is not wholly abandoned. In it is an arousal of longing and an incitement to know it. It completes his words "ask," and is an indication that he is innocent of what he was accused of, by appealing to God's knowledge of it. In it is also a warning to them for their plotting, and that God will requite them for it. His saying:

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[51] ﴿He said, "What was your business when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said, "Allah forbid! We know of no evil in him." The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾

﴿He said, "What was your business when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?"﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) constructed in response to a question, as if it were said: "What happened after that?" So it is said: The king said, "What was your business", i.e., what was your matter, "when you sought to seduce Joseph on the day of the banquet?" That is: Did you find any inclination in him toward you?

﴿They said, "Allah forbid! We know of no evil in him."﴾ That is, no ugliness. They went to the utmost in negating its kind from him by using the indefinite form (nakirah) and the addition of (min) ﴿من﴾. ﴿The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become evident."﴾ That is, it was established, settled, and manifested after being hidden. ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful.﴾ That is, in his saying: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾ [Yusuf: 26].

Al-Zamakhshari said: There is no addition to their testimony to his innocence and purity, and their acknowledgment against themselves, that he had not been involved in anything of what they had accused him of; for they were his adversaries. When the adversary acknowledges that his opponent is in the right and he himself is in the wrong, no one has any further argument. End of quote.

؎ And excellence is what even the enemies testify to.

(p-٣٥٥٣) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[52] ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret, and that Allah does not guide the plotting of the treacherous.﴾

﴿That﴾: The wife of the Chief says: "That is the thing I have acknowledged against myself, ﴿so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾" — that is, so that Yusuf may know that I did not lie about him in his absence, and that I have come with the truth and sincerity concerning what I was asked about. Or it means: so that my husband may know that I did not betray him in secret in reality, and that the greatest transgression did not occur; rather, I only solicited this young man, he refused, and so I confessed, so that he may know that I am innocent.

﴿And that Allah does not guide the plotting of the treacherous﴾ — that is, He does not approve of it, nor does He make it succeed.

The commentary on His saying, the Exalted:

[53] ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent commander of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent commander of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ She means: "And I do not absolve myself despite that, for the soul speaks to itself and desires, and for this reason I solicited him." Or it means: "I do not absolve myself of betrayal, for I betrayed him when I accused him and said: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your wife except that he be imprisoned?﴾ [Yusuf: 25], and I put him in prison." She intends by this an apology for what she had done: that every soul is a persistent commander of evil, except a soul upon which Allah has shown mercy by protecting it from sin, like the soul of Yusuf.

Then, regarding the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is so that he may know﴾ [Yusuf: 52], and the rest of the verse, on the basis that it is a report of the statement of the wife of the Aziz, Ibn Kathir said: this is the most well-known opinion, the most fitting and the most appropriate to the context of the story and the meanings of the speech. Al-Mawardi related it in his tafsir, and Imam Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, undertook to defend it and devoted to it a separate work. It has been said that this is from the speech of Yusuf, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related no other than this. The meaning is: that deliberation, carefulness and diligence were for the manifestation of innocence, so that the Aziz would know that I did not betray him in his household in his absence; or so that Allah would know that I did not betray him, because sin is a form of betrayal. Then he affirmed his trustworthiness by His saying: (p-3554) ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾ [Yusuf: 52], and that if he had been a betrayer, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, would not have guided his affair, meaning: would not have made it upright and made its outcome good. Within this is an indirect allusion to the wife of the Aziz in her betrayal of his trust, and to the Aziz in his betrayal of the trust of Allah, the Exalted, when he supported her after the signs had become apparent in imprisoning him. Then he wished to humble himself before Allah and to abase his own self, lest he be one who praises himself for her, or one who is pleased and proud of his own trustworthiness. And to make clear that the trustworthiness in him was not from himself alone, but was by the success, kindness and protection of Allah. So he said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾, meaning: I do not declare it free of error, nor do I testify to it for complete innocence, nor do I purify it, for the human soul commands evil and drives toward it by the desires within it, except for those souls upon which Allah has shown mercy, which He protects from falling into wrongdoing.

This is the summary of what they established on the basis that it is from the speech of Yusuf. Ibn Kathir said: the first opinion is stronger and more evident, because the context of the whole speech is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz in the presence of the king, and Yusuf, peace be upon him, was not with them; rather, after that the king had him brought. And Allah knows best.

Subtleties:

The first: the position of His saying (bil-ghayb) "in the unseen" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject or the object, meaning: "while I was absent from him, or while she was absent from him, or while he was absent from me and hidden from my sight." Or it is an adverbial of place, meaning: in the place of the unseen, which is concealment and hiding behind the doors.

The second: it has been said that the meaning of ﴿Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾ [Yusuf: 52] is: He does not guide them through their plotting. The negated guidance was attributed to the plot, while it actually applies to them, as a figurative usage for emphasis, because when the cause is not guided, it is known that its causer is even less guided.

It has also been said: the meaning is that He does not guide them in their plotting, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They imitate the saying of those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], meaning: in their saying.

And it has been said: guiding the plot is a metaphor for its execution and its being made firm.

The third: Al-Alusi said in (al-Iklil): ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾ is a basis for humility and the breaking and abasement of the self.

The fourth: Al-Zamakhshari said: The falsifiers have fabricated fabricated narrations, then he cited them and said: and this is due to their eagerness to slander Allah and His messengers.

Al-Nasir said: He has indeed spoken truthfully about the accusation against those who transmitted these additions as slander, and that is the way of the falsifiers from every group. And Allah establishes the truth by His words and nullifies falsehood.

The fifth: I have seen in Ibn al-Qayyim's (al-Jawab al-Kafi), concerning the wondrous patience and chastity of Yusuf in the face of the pressures, from several aspects. He, may mercy be upon him, after laying down an introduction on the corruptions of love for beautiful forms, both immediate and deferred, said: they are many times what any reminder mentions, for it corrupts the heart in essence, and when the heart is corrupted, wills, speech and deeds are corrupted, and the foundation of monotheism is corrupted. Allah, the Exalted, only related this illness concerning two groups of people: the people of Lot and women. He informed of the love of the wife of the Aziz for Yusuf, and what she solicited him with, and how she plotted against him with it; and He informed of the state to which Yusuf came because of his patience, chastity and piety, although what he was tested with is a matter that none can endure except one whom Allah has made patient. For the carrying out of an action corresponds to the strength of the motive and the removal of the obstacle, and the motive here was at its utmost strength, for several reasons:

The first: what Allah, glorified is He, placed in the nature of man of inclination toward women, as the thirsty incline toward water and the hungry toward food, to the point that many people can endure without food and drink but cannot endure without women. This is not blameworthy when it encounters what is lawful; rather, it is praiseworthy.

The second: Yusuf, peace be upon him, was a young man, and the desire of youth and its intensity are stronger.

The third: he was unmarried, with no wife and no concubine to break the intensity of desire.

The fourth: he was in a land of strangeness, where a stranger can obtain satisfaction there that is not obtainable for others in their homeland, among their family and acquaintances.

(p-3556) The fifth: the woman had rank and beauty, such that each of these two matters calls to intercourse with her.

The sixth: she was not refusing nor unwilling, for many people lose their desire for a woman through her refusal and unwillingness, because of the humiliation of submission and asking that they feel within themselves; and many people's love increases by refusal and unwillingness, as the poet said:

"Love's longing increased in me when it was denied to me: the thing most beloved to man is that which is forbidden."

People's natures differ in this. Some have their love multiplied when a woman gives herself and desires, and it dwindles when she refuses and withholds; and some have their love and will multiplied by prohibition, and their longing intensifies with everything that is forbidden, and they obtain from the pleasure of victory a likeness of the pleasure of victory after her refusal and aversion. And the pleasure lies in attaining a matter after its difficulty, and in the intensity of eagerness to attain it.

The seventh: she sought, desired and exerted effort, so she spared him the burden of seeking and the humiliation of desiring her; rather, she was the desirous one, humbled, and he was the honored one who was desired.

The eighth: he was in her house, under her authority and domination, such that he feared, if he did not obey her, harm from her; so the motive of desire and the motive of fear gathered together.

The ninth: he did not fear that she would slander him, nor that anyone from her side would, for she was the seeker and the desirer, and she had locked the doors and hidden the watchers.

The tenth: he had been her slave in the house, such that he would enter and leave and be present with her, and no one would object to him; and intimacy preceded the seeking, and it is among the strongest motives, as was said to an Arab woman: "What drove you to such-and-such?" She said: "The nearness of the cushion and the length of the night." She meant: the nearness of the man's cushion to my cushion, and the length of the night between us.

The eleventh: she sought help against him from masters of deceit and cunning, and showed him them, and complained of her state to them, so that they would help her against him; then he sought help from Allah against them, and said: ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I would incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 33].

The twelfth: she threatened him with prison and humiliation, and this is a kind of coercion, for it is a threat from one who is likely to carry it out, so the motive of desire and the motive of safety gathered together, out of fear of the narrowness of prison and humiliation.

The thirteenth: the husband did not show any jealousy or strength that would separate them and distance each of them from the other; rather, the most he said to them was that he said to Yusuf: "Turn away from this," and to the woman: "Ask forgiveness for your sin, for you were among the sinners." Strong jealousy in a man is among the strongest obstacles, and here no jealousy appeared from him.

Despite these motives, he preferred the pleasure of Allah and His fear, and his love for Allah led him to choose prison over fornication, so he said: ﴿My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. He knew that he could not turn that away from himself, and that if his Lord did not protect him and turn away from him their plot, he would incline to them by his nature and would be among the ignorant. This is from the perfection of his knowledge of his Lord and of himself. In this story are lessons, benefits and wisdoms that exceed a thousand benefits. End of Ibn al-Qayyim's words.

Then the Exalted pointed to what He bestowed upon Yusuf in raising his rank through his patience, and elevating his station through His mercy, by His saying, glorified is He:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[54] ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself."  So when he had spoken with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trustworthy in our presence."﴾

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself."﴾ That is, I will single him out for myself, apart from al-'Aziz, following the custom of kings in reserving what is precious and distinguished. He said this when he had confirmed his innocence of what was attributed to him, and his nobility of character and breadth of knowledge. ﴿So when he had spoken with him﴾, that is, when they brought him and he spoke with him—that is, the king addressed him and came to know him, and witnessed his excellence, wisdom and innocence. (It is permissible that the subject of "spoke with him" be Yusuf, peace be upon him.) ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are today established in rank and position in our presence"﴾, that is, possessed of standing and station, ﴿and trustworthy﴾, that is, entrusted with everything.

It is related that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, came before the king and interpreted his dream for him, the king rejoiced in his speech, he and his close companions, and said to them: "Do we find another man like him, one through whom divine support descends?" And he said to Yusuf: "After God has made you know this, there is no one as wise as you. You are over my house, and my subjects submit to your word. I shall not be greater than you except through my throne, and I have appointed you over the entire land of Egypt." He took his ring from his hand, placed it on his finger, dressed him in garments of fine silk, placed a gold necklace around his neck, mounted him in his chariot, and ordered that he be paraded through the streets of Egypt, with proclamations of submission to him before him. The king said to him: "No matter shall proceed and no affair shall be executed in Egypt except by your opinion and counsel." He named him "Savior of the World" and married him to the daughter of one of the great men of his court. Yusuf was then thirty years old—and God knows best.

Some have said: Whoever reflects deeply on the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, knows with certainty that God does not waste the effort of the pious and trustworthy person, but rather makes his end good and elevates his station in this world and the Hereafter; and that one who holds fast to patience does not fear the vicissitudes of time and its trials, nor fear its calamities and misfortunes, for God supports him, makes his endeavor succeed, and perpetuates his fragrant remembrance through the passage of ages. For when Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not fear the threats of calamities, nor fear the tests of trials as a menace, and did not fear oppression and evil from prison, nor harm and pain from being tortured, but cast his trust upon the Lord and endured that affliction with a steadfast heart, he attained, through his purity and piety, the crown of honor and a tongue of truthfulness throughout the days of time. Indeed, his excellence has not had its lovely memory effaced by the passing of days, nor has the recurrence of years toyed with its freshness; rather, it has been stored up for us as an example whose footsteps we follow when trials befall us, a refuge to which we turn in tribulations and calamities, and a model whose path we train ourselves to follow in steadfastness at moments of stumbling, and whose way of piety and goodly garment we adopt. Thus we attain in this world the mark of glory, and in the Hereafter we win the abode of eternity.

And His words, Exalted is He:

(p-3559) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Saying, Exalted is He:

[55] ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾

﴿He said﴾, that is, Joseph said to the king, ﴿"Appoint me over the treasuries of the land"﴾, that is, put me in charge of the treasuries of your land, meaning all the harvests for the years they would face, the years about which he had informed them, so that he might manage them for them in the most rightly guided and beneficial way. Then he showed his capability in this matter, saying, ﴿"Indeed, I am a knowing guardian"﴾, that is, a trustworthy one who guards what you entrust to me, and one who knows the ways of managing it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He described himself with trustworthiness and competence, the two qualities that kings seek in those whom they appoint.

He only said this so that he could reach the enforcement of God Exalted's rulings, the establishment of truth, the spreading of justice, and the empowerment to do that for which prophets are sent to the servants. He knew that no one other than himself could fill his place in this, so he sought the appointment seeking the face of God, not out of love for kingship and worldly life.

If you ask: How was it permissible for him to take up a position from the hand of an unbeliever, and to be subordinate to him and under his command and obedience?

I say: Mujahid narrated that he had indeed embraced Islam. And on the authority of Qatada: it is evidence that a person may take up a position from the hand of an oppressive ruler. The early pious predecessors (al-salaf) used to take up judgeship from the side of usurpers (al-baghat) and considered it permissible. And if a prophet or a scholar knows that there is no way to rule by God's command and to repel injustice except by empowering a disbelieving or wicked king, then he may seek support through him.

It has also been said: the king used to act upon his opinion and would not object to him in everything he saw, so he was in the position of one who follows and obeys him. End of quotation.

This verse is a foundation for seeking authority, such as judgeship and similar posts, for one who is confident in himself to fulfill its duties, and for the permissibility of accepting appointment from an unbeliever or an oppressor. It is also a foundation for the permissibility of a person praising himself for the sake of a benefit, and for the principle that one who takes up a matter should be knowledgeable about it, experienced, and sharp in understanding. Thus said (al-Iklil).

Abu al-Su'ud said: He did not mention the king's agreement to what Joseph, peace be upon him, requested, namely appointing him over the treasuries of the land, as a sign that this is a matter that cannot be refused, needing no explicit statement, especially after mentioning what falls under it of the full rights of rulership, in His saying: ﴿"Indeed, today you are established and trusted in our sight"﴾ [Yusuf: 54], and as an alert that all of this is from God, Mighty and Majestic, and that the king was only a means in it.

Note:

Ibn Kathir said: "The treasuries of the land are the pyramids, in which the harvests were gathered....etc."

I have not yet found the source for the claim that the pyramids were the place where the harvests were gathered, nor have I found it in the words of anyone else.

"Al-Ahram" (the pyramids), with a fatha on the hamza, is the plural of haram (with fatha on both letters). They are square-based, pyramid-shaped structures. Three of them remain today at Giza, several miles from Cairo, counted among the wonders of the world. I was invited to see them during my journey to the land of Egypt in the year 1321 AH. The opinion of the later scholars regarding their true purpose has settled on their having been tombs for their kings.

In the book (Al-Athar al-Jalil li-Qudama' Wadi al-Nil): All the pyramids are nothing but royal tombs, whose owners preferred to be distinguished by them after death from other people, just as they were distinguished from them during their lives, and they intended that their remembrance through them would endure across long ages and distant eras. The historians of this age have agreed that the Great Pyramid is the tomb of the king Khufu, the second of Khafre, and the third of the king Menkaure, all of them from the Fourth Dynasty. There is no weight to the claim of those who assert that they were temples, or observatories for the stars, or a school for priestly knowledge, or other than that. End of quotation.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary on His words, exalted is He:

[56] ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle in it wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾

﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt. ﴿To settle in it﴾, i.e., to dwell (p-3561) in whatever part of its territories he wished, ﴿wherever he willed﴾. That is because when he (peace be upon him) was appointed over the treasuries of Egypt, he traveled through its regions and toured its villages, while the command was his command and the directive was his directive, by the care and mercy of Him, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost﴾, i.e., those who did good deeds.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[57] ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾ That is: its reward is better than the reward of this world for the believers who are mindful of God. It is an indication that the highest aim is the reward of the Hereafter, and that what is stored up for these people is greater and more majestic than what they are granted in this world of establishment in the land, status, wealth, and dominion.

Discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[58] ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.﴾

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.﴾ This refers to the fulfillment of Joseph's dream. The matter was that the land became fertile for seven years, and it brought forth from its blessings an amount equal to the sand of the sea in abundance. Joseph gathered its grain and placed in every city the grain of the fields around it. When these seven years had passed, the lean years set in, and the drought spread over Egypt, Syria and their surrounding regions. The people from all the lands began to travel to Egypt to obtain grain (mirah) for themselves and their families, because they knew that food was available there. Among those who set out to seek grain were the brothers of Joseph, at the command of their father Ya'qub (Jacob), because the drought had reached their land, Palestine. They rode out in a group of ten men, while Ya'qub kept his son Benjamin, Joseph's full brother, with him, fearing that some harm might befall him; he was the dearest of his sons to him after Joseph. When they descended upon Egypt, they entered upon Joseph, but they did not recognize him, because of the long time that had passed and their parting from him when he was young, and because they never imagined that he would come to what he had come to. As for him, he recognized them. It is narrated that when they entered upon him (p-3562) they prostrated to him with their faces to the ground, as a greeting to him. He then began to address them while disguising himself from them, and said: "Where have you come from?" They said: "From the land of Kan'an, to buy food." He said to them: "You are spies; you have only come to spy out the borders of the land." They said: "God forbid! Your servants have come only for grain, because hardship has struck us, and we are brothers, sons of one father." He said: "How many are you?" They said: "We were twelve; one of us has perished." He said: "How many are you here?" They said: "Ten." He said: "Where is the eleventh brother?" They said: "He is with his father, who finds comfort in him for the one who was lost." He said: "There is no escape from testing the truth of your words. Let one of you remain with me as a pledge, and let the rest of you go and take grain for the famine of your families, and bring your younger brother to me, so that your truthfulness may be confirmed." Then he seized Simeon, kept him with him, permitted the rest to leave, and commanded that they be given provisions for the journey. This is what is alluded to in His words, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[59] ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?"﴾

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾ — with a fatḥah on the jīm (jahhazahum), and it is also read with a kasrah, meaning: he loaded their camels with food and provisions. ﴿He said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure﴾ — i.e., I complete it — ﴿and that I am the best of hosts﴾ — i.e., the best of those who entertain guests." His saying that is an incitement for them to bring him, not a boast of favour.

The commentary on the Almighty's words:

[60] ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (of grain) for you with me, and you shall not come near me.﴾

﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (of grain) for you with me﴾ means: in what is yet to come. ﴿And you shall not come near me﴾ means: and you shall not bring me near by entering my land a second time. The yā' (the first-person pronoun) is elided, and the nūn is the nūn al-wiqāya (the protective nūn, a nūn inserted before the verb's final yā' suffix to protect the verb's ending from being broken by kasra).

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿They said, "We will seek to get him from his father, and indeed we will do it."﴾

﴿They said, "We will seek to get him from his father"﴾ means: we will deceive him and devise a scheme to pry him away from his hand, and we will exert effort in that. In this there is an indication of how difficult the request is and how hard it is to attain, as said by Abu al-Su'ud. ﴿And indeed we will do it﴾ means: that. They mean the seeking (al-murawadah), or bringing him back, so it is an escalation to a promise of achieving it after the seeking.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[62] ﴿And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, that perhaps they will come back."﴾

﴿And he said to his servants﴾, i.e., to his attendants who measured out the grain: ﴿Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags﴾, meaning by "their merchandise" the goods with which they bought the food. It is related that it was silver. I.e., put it into their baggage from where they will not notice. ﴿So that they may recognize it﴾, i.e., in order that they may recognize it, ﴿when they return to their family﴾, i.e., and open their bags, ﴿that perhaps they will come back﴾, i.e., as you have ordered them to do; for the bestowal of favour upon them by giving back the two portions is among the strongest incentives to returning.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[63] ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may measure [provisions], and indeed we will be his guardians."﴾

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us"﴾ That is: we were warned that it would be withheld from us from now on, if we do not bring our brother. ﴿So send with us our brother, that we may measure﴾ That is, we remove the impediment to measure and take from the food what we need. It was also read as (yakta'il) ﴿يَكْتَلْ﴾ with a "ya" (third person), meaning: our brother will measure for himself along with our measuring. ﴿And indeed we will be his guardians﴾ That is, from any harm reaching him.

(p-3564) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[64] ﴿He said, "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Ya'qub (Jacob) said to them, ﴿"Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before?"﴾, i.e., before him, Yusuf (Joseph). He means: "Can I take from you a covenant and a pledge greater than what I took from you concerning Yusuf, when you said, 'Indeed, we will surely be his guardians'? Then you betrayed your guarantee. So what assures me against the like of that? I do not trust you, nor your guarding, and I only entrust the matter to Allah." ﴿"So Allah is the best guardian"﴾, i.e., better than you and better than everyone else, ﴿"and He is the most merciful of the merciful"﴾, i.e., more merciful than his parents and his brothers. So I hope that He will show mercy to me by guarding him. This is an inclination on his part toward permitting them to take him with them, because of the benefit he saw in it.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[65] ﴿When they opened their belongings and found their merchandise (bidaa'atahum) returned to them, they said: "O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an extra camel-load. That is an easy measure."﴾

﴿When they opened their belongings and found their merchandise returned to them﴾ means: they found their silver coins (darahimahum), the price of their food, in their belongings.

It is narrated that one of them opened his bag to take fodder for his animal, and saw his silver in the mouth of his bag. He said to his brothers: "My silver has been returned, and here it is in my bag." Then, when they reached Kan'an and began emptying their sacks, each of them found the bundle of his silver in his sack. Their hearts were stirred, they were astonished, and they praised God's care for them.

﴿They said: "O our father, what more could we desire?"﴾ means: what could we seek beyond this? Is there any further increase? That is, there is no addition to what he has done, for he has honored us, treated us well in our lodging, and returned the price to us. The intent was to win him over from his opinion. Or: we do not seek to speak falsely, nor do we lie in what we have related to you of his kindness, which calls us to obey his command. Or: we do not seek, and we speak only the truth, in what we advise you regarding sending us back with our brother. It is also read in the second person (al-khitab), meaning: what more do you seek beyond this as proof of our truthfulness?

﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustaanifah) clarifying what the denial implies, namely that the kindness has reached its utmost limit. It is as if they said: how could it not be so, when this is our merchandise, returned to us out of bounty from a direction we did not expect?

﴿And we will bring provisions for our family﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with an understood implied element. That is: so we will rely on it, and bring provisions for our family when we return to the king. Mirah means to bring food, as in the expression "māra-hu" (he brought him food). From this comes the saying: "ma 'indahu khayrun wa la mayrun" (he has neither goodness nor provision).

﴿And guard our brother﴾ means: so that nothing befalls him of what you fear. ﴿And gain an extra camel-load﴾ means: by taking him with us. ﴿That is an easy measure﴾ means: easy for this king who is generous in his munificence, so he will not burden us regarding it. Or the meaning is: short in duration; it is not the way of such a matter that its period should be lengthened by detention and delay. Or the meaning is: what is measured out for us without our brother is a small, meagre thing, so send our brother with us that we may be enlarged and increased by its measure...

Ibn Kathir said: this is part of the speech and its embellishment. That is, this (amount) is small in comparison with the taking of their brother, and it does not equal it; so it is not part of their speech. The sentence admits of both readings.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

[66] ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in Allah's name that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded (overcome)." And when they had given their solemn pledge, he said, "Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾

﴿He said﴾: that is, their father said to them. ﴿I will never send him with you﴾: that is, with this statement. ﴿until you give me a solemn covenant in Allah's name that you will surely bring him back to me﴾: that is, a pledge from Him and an oath by Him that you will return him to me. ﴿unless you are surrounded (yuhata bikum)﴾: that is, all of you are overpowered, so that you are unable to free him. Its root is from "the enemy surrounded him" (ahata bihi al-'aduww), meaning he blocked his paths of escape and his destruction drew near.

﴿And when they had given their solemn pledge, he said, "Allah is Witness (wakil) over what we say"﴾: that is, a witness and a watchful guardian. The purpose is to urge them to keep their pledge by frightening them about breaking it, through His requiting them.

Ibn Ishaq said: He only did this because he had no choice but to send them for the sake of the provision (al-mirah), on which they could not do without.

A Subtle Point:

al-Nasir said: This story has indeed confirmed the well-known proverb, which is their saying: "Calamity is entrusted to speech" (al-bala' mawkul bi'l-mantiq). For Ya'qub, peace be upon him, first said regarding Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], and he was tested through this statement. And here he said a second time: ﴿unless you are surrounded (yuhata bikum)﴾, that is, you are overcome. So he was tested by that as well, and they were surrounded and overcome. End of quote.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[67] ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates. Yet I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Judgment is only for Allah. upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely [indeed] rely."﴾

﴿And he said﴾, i.e., their father: ﴿"O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates"﴾, i.e., so that their entering through one gate would not draw the attention of those of the soldiers stationed there, and of the one who patrols for the ruler (al-'assas), so that he would become suspicious of them. For a group entering in one form and one uniform, as strangers to that land, attracts the attention of every watcher. At that time cities were gated, and no one could enter them except through their gates, and each gate had its guards. The entry of an individual is not like the entry of a group in arousing alertness and the following of the eye. It was also said: he forbade them lest the evil eye (al-'ayn) afflict them if they entered as one troop (kawkaba wahida), and its explanation will come.

﴿"Yet I cannot avail you anything against Allah"﴾, i.e., I cannot repel from you, by my planning, anything of what has been decreed for you, for caution does not prevent destiny (al-qadar).

Abu al-Su'ud said: He, peace be upon him, did not intend by this the complete nullification of caution, how could he, when He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and He says: ﴿Take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 71]. Rather, he intended to clarify that what he enjoined upon them is not something that necessarily brings about the intended outcome, but is rather a measure taken in general. The effect and the bringing about of benefit through it come only from the Mighty, the All-Powerful. This is not a repelling of destiny, but rather seeking help from Allah, Exalted is He, and fleeing to Him from Him.

﴿"Judgment is only for Allah"﴾, i.e., none shares in it with Him, and nothing can obstruct Him. ﴿"upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely [indeed] rely."﴾

[p. 3568] The explanation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[68] ﴿When they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them against Allah at all; it was only a need within Ya'qub's soul, which he fulfilled. And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.﴾

﴿When they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ — that is, from the separate gates. ﴿It did not avail them against Allah at all﴾ — that is, that entering did not avail them. ﴿It was only a need within Ya'qub's soul, which he fulfilled﴾ — that is, which he expressed. ﴿And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾ — that is, a possessor of great knowledge, owing to Our teaching him through revelation and the establishing of proofs, since he did not believe that caution repels decree, nor that planning has any share in causing effect. In the emphasis of the sentence by ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) and the lam of emphasis, the indefinite form of ﴿knowledge﴾, and in attributing its cause to teaching that is ascribed to His own Essence, glorified is He, there is an indication of Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) station and of the high rank and magnitude of his knowledge, which is not hidden — as Abu al-Su'ud stated.

﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ — that is, so they assume that the means are causes that produce effects.

Ibn Hazm said in *al-Milal*: Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) command to them to enter by separate gates was out of concern for them, either from the evil eye, or from the attack of an enemy, or from a suspicious person who might gather against them, or from something else that frightened him for them. He (peace be upon him) acknowledged that his doing that and his commanding them to do it did not avail them against Allah at all, if He, Mighty and Majestic, willed something for them. But since the nature of human beings applied to Ya'qub (peace be upon him) and to all the prophets (peace be upon them), as Allah, Exalted is He, related about the messengers that they said: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 11], this led him to a certain light consideration that eased the soul's need, its tugging, and its longing for the safety of someone it loves — although that does not avail anything at all — just as he (peace be upon him) used to love a good omen.

Note:

As-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: In this verse — according to what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others — the evil eye is real, and caution does not repel decree. Nevertheless, one must still take account of the means. End of quotation.

Some Yemeni scholars said: This passage has fruits, namely: the recommendation to keep away from the harms of people and to be cautious of them. But as for Allah's action, caution does not avert it. Then he said: In *al-Tahdhib* it is stated that Abu 'Ali denied that the evil eye causes harm, and this is also reported from a group of the theologians (mutakallimun).

Al-Hakim, al-Amir al-Husayn and others affirmed the permissibility of that, on the basis of reports that came concerning it.

[p. 3569] Then he said: It has been disputed from where the harm produced by the evil eye comes. Some say that a ray issues from the eye of the one who gives the evil eye, reaches the one who sees it, and affects him like poison. Al-Hakim rejected this, saying that if it were so, it would not be specific to some things and not others, and because substances are alike, so one of them would not affect another. Others say that it is the action of the one who gives the evil eye. He said: This is not correct, because a body does not act upon another body except through contact, or what is in its category of impingements, and because if he were doing it, it would depend on his choice. Others say that it is the action of Allah: Allah has made it a custom for such an effect as a form of correction. Al-Hakim affirmed this, and it is what al-Zamakhshari and al-Amir al-Husayn mentioned, and it is the view of Abu Hashim. He reported it from them in *al-Tahdhib*. End of quotation.

Al-Razi clarified this by saying: Abu Hashim and Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi said: It is not impossible that the evil eye is real, and its meaning is that the one who has the evil eye, when he sees a thing and is impressed by it with admiration, the benefit for him in his being obligated is that Allah changes that person and that thing, so that the heart of that obligated one no longer remains attached to it. This meaning is not impossible. Then it is also not far-fetched that if he mentions his Lord at that moment, turns away from admiration, and asks his Lord to protect him from that, then the benefit becomes determined by that. And since this custom is consistent, it is rightly said: the evil eye is real. End of quotation.

I say: Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, in *Zad al-Ma'ad*, has expounded this subject in a way that satisfies and suffices, in the section on the Prophet's (ﷺ) guidance regarding the treatment of the evil eye, after mentioning what is reported in the two Sahihs and others concerning the reality of the evil eye and the fame of its effect among the Arabs. He said:

A group of those whose share of revelation and reason is small denied the matter of the evil eye and said: It is only imaginings with no reality. These are among the most ignorant of people in revelation and reason, the most veiled in their understanding, the most dense in their natures, and the farthest from knowledge of the spirits and souls, their attributes, their actions and their effects. The reasonable nations, despite the differences of their religions and sects, do not reject the matter of the evil eye or deny it, though they differ [p. 3570] about its cause and the manner of its effect. One group said: When the soul of the one who gives the evil eye is disposed in a bad condition, a poisonous force issues from his eye and reaches the one he gazes upon, and he is harmed. They said: This is no more strange than a poisonous force issuing from a snake and reaching a human being, so that he dies. It is well known of one kind of snake that if its gaze falls upon a human being, he dies; likewise the one who gives the evil eye.

Another group said: It is not unlikely that from the eyes of some people subtle substances issue that are not seen, reach the one gazed upon, penetrate the pores of his body, and harm results for him.

Another group said: Allah has made it a custom to create whatever harm He wills when the eye of the one who gives the evil eye faces the one he afflicts, without there being in him any force, cause or influence at all. This is the doctrine of those who deny causes, forces and effects in the world. These people have closed for themselves the door of causes, effects and means, and they have opposed all reasonable people. There is no doubt that Allah, glorified is He, created in bodies and spirits various forces and natures, and placed in many of them properties and influential qualities. A reasonable person cannot deny the influence of spirits upon bodies, for this is a matter observed and sensed. You see how a face reddens intensely when someone whom it respects and is shy before looks at it, and how it turns intensely pale at the gaze of one it fears. People have witnessed one who falls ill from a look, and whose strength weakens; all of this is through the influence of spirits, and because of the intensity of their connection with the eye the act is attributed to it, though it is not the agent; the influence belongs to the spirit. Spirits differ in their natures, forces, qualities and properties. The spirit of the envier harms the envied with clear harm, and for this reason Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to seek refuge in Him from its evil. The influence of the envier on the harm of the envied is something that none denies except one who has left the reality of humanity, and it is the root of striking by the evil eye, for the wicked envious soul takes on a wicked condition that confronts the envied and affects him through that property. The most similar thing to this is the snake, for its poison is latent within it in potential; when it confronts its enemy, a wrathful force issues from it, and its soul takes on a harmful wicked condition. Of these, some grow intense in their condition and become strong enough to affect the miscarriage of the fetus, and some affect the blinding of the sight. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the cut-tailed snake and the two-striped snake: ««They both seek out the sight and cause miscarriage»». [p. 3571] Some affect the human being by the mere sight of their condition, without contact, because of the great wickedness of that soul and its harmful wicked condition. The influence is not restricted to bodily contacts, as he who has little knowledge of nature and of the Law supposes; rather, influence occurs sometimes by contact, sometimes by confrontation, sometimes by sight, sometimes by the spirit's turning toward the one it affects, and sometimes by supplications, incantations and seeking refuge, and sometimes by imagination and fancy. The influence of the one who gives the evil eye does not depend on sight; he may be blind, and something is described to him, and his soul affects it even though he has not seen it. Many who give the evil eye affect the one they afflict by description without seeing him. Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you with their eyes﴾ [al-Qalam: 51], and He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak, from the evil of what He created, and from the evil of darkness when it settles, and from the evil of the blowers in knots, and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾ [al-Falaq: 1–5]. So every evil-eye giver is an envier, but not every envier is an evil-eye giver. Since the envier is more general than the one who gives the evil eye, seeking refuge from him is seeking refuge from the evil eye as well. These are arrows that issue from the soul of the envier and from the eye toward the envied and the afflicted: the eye strikes him sometimes and misses him sometimes. If it finds him exposed with no protection upon him, it certainly affects him; and if it finds him cautious, armed, with no opening for the arrows, it does not affect him, and it may even return the arrows to their owner. This is exactly like the sensible throwing of an object: this belongs to souls and spirits, and that belongs to bodies and forms. Its root is the admiration of the one who gives the evil eye for a thing, then his wicked condition follows it, and then he seeks to carry out its poison by a look at the one afflicted. A man may give the evil eye to himself, and he may give it without intending to, by his nature. This is the worst kind of human affliction. Our companions and other jurists have said: whoever is known for this, the Imam shall imprison him and provide for him what is spent upon him until death. This is certainly the correct view. End of Ibn al-Qayyim's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Al-Razi said: It is not a condition of an agent that its influence be according to sensible qualities, namely heat, cold, moisture and dryness; rather the influence may be purely psychological, with no connection to bodily powers. What shows this is that a plank that is narrow in width, when placed on the ground, a person can walk on it, but if it were placed between two high walls, a person would be unable to walk on it. This is only because his fear of falling from it causes him to fall. So we know that psychological impressions exist.

Also, when a person imagines that someone is harming him, anger arises in his heart and his temperament heats up greatly; the source of that heat is none other than that psychological imagining. And since the source of bodily movements is none other than psychological perceptions, when it is established that the soul's perception causes a change in its particular body, it is not far-fetched that some souls are such that their influences extend to other bodies. Thus it is established that it is not impossible in reason that the soul affects other bodies. Also, the substances of souls differ in their essence, so it is not impossible that some souls are such that they affect the change of another living being's body, on condition that they see it and marvel at it. Thus it is established that this meaning is a possibility, and experiences from ancient times support it, and prophetic souls have spoken of it. Therefore, no doubt about its occurrence remains for one who knows this. When this is established, it is established that what the earlier exegetes (mufassirun) agreed upon in interpreting this verse as referring to striking by the evil eye is a true statement that cannot be rejected. End of quotation.

(p-3573) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[69] ﴿And when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself. He said: "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not be distressed by what they used to do."﴾

Glorified is He, informs that when the brothers of Joseph came before him, he took his brother Benjamin to himself, either at the meal or in the dwelling, and informed him that he was his brother, and said to him: "Do not be distressed" — that is, do not grieve over what they did to us in the past, for God Most High has been good to us and has gathered us with goodness.

It has been narrated that when they came to him and stood before him, he saw his brother Benjamin with them, so he commanded that they be lodged in his house, dwelling in his honour and hospitality, and attending with him at his midday meal. Then he entered upon them, and they stood and prostrated to him, and he asked them about the wellbeing of their father. He raised his gaze to his brother, drew him near, took him to himself, and made him at ease with his conversation — as mentioned in the verse. Then Joseph wished to devise a way to keep his brother with him, so he came to an agreement with his servants, when he equipped his brothers, that they should put his drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag, as God Most High explained with His words:

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[70] ﴿Then when he had furnished them with their provisions, he put the drinking-cup into his brother's bag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are thieves!"﴾

﴿When he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, i.e., of the food, ﴿he put the drinking-cup into his brother's bag﴾. It was a silver goblet from which Yusuf used to drink, and he placed it in his brother's supplies.

It has been related that when Yusuf had equipped them and they had set off, he allowed them time until they had departed and gone a short distance from the city. Then he commanded that they be pursued and be informed of what was missing, as Allah the Exalted indicated by His saying: ﴿Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are thieves!"﴾

(p-3574) The interpretation of His, the Exalted, words:

[71] ﴿They said, turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ [72] ﴿They said, "We are missing the king's goblet, and for whoever brings it is a camel-load, and I am its guarantor."﴾ [Yusuf: 72]

﴿They said, turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾

﴿They said, "We are missing the king's goblet, and for whoever brings it is a camel-load, and I am its guarantor."﴾ [Yusuf: 72] The meaning of (adhdhana) is "called out." It is said: "adhdhanahu" means "informed him," and "adhdhana" means "gave much notice." From this comes (al-mu'adhdhin), the caller, because of how often he does this.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[73] ﴿They said: By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and that we are not thieves.﴾

﴿They said: By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and that we are not thieves.﴾ That is: we did not come for theft, nor for corruption of any kind; we came only for provisions (al-mirah), and we were never described as thieves. They called upon their own knowledge as proof of their innocence, because of what they were certain of concerning their own condition during their two visits.

(p-3575) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿They said: "What then is the penalty for it, if you are liars?"﴾ [75] ﴿They said: "Its penalty is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its penalty. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers."﴾ [Yusuf: 74–75].

﴿They said, "What then is the penalty for it"﴾, i.e., for the thief, ﴿"if you are liars?"﴾

﴿They said﴾ [Yusuf: 75], i.e., trusting in their own innocence: ﴿"Its penalty is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its penalty"﴾ [Yusuf: 75], i.e., the penalty for his theft is that whoever is found in his baggage is taken as a slave. The words ﴿"he himself is its penalty"﴾ [Yusuf: 75] are an affirmation of that ruling and its binding force, meaning: seizing him is his penalty and no other. It is also permissible that "its penalty" (jaza'uhu) be the subject (mubtada'), and the conditional clause be its predicate (khabar) as it stands, by placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun; the original would be "its penalty is: whoever is found in his baggage, he is it." ﴿"Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers"﴾ [Yusuf: 75], i.e., for theft. It is an emphasis upon emphasis, and an explanation of the ugliness of theft.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[76] ﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed. We raise by degrees whom We will, and over every possessor of knowledge is One who knows.﴾

﴿He began﴾, that is, Joseph's servant (fatā) ﴿with their bags﴾, that is, he searched them ﴿before the bag of his brother﴾, that is, Binyamin, to clear himself of accusation. ﴿Then he brought it out﴾, that is, the drinking-bowl (al-siqāya), ﴿from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph﴾, that is, We arranged the means to attain his purpose. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾, that is, under his statute and legislation (dīn, here meaning law). This clause is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) and a causal explanation (ta'līl) of that scheme and its contrivance. That is: it was not right for him to take his brother under the king's judgment, so God, exalted is He, arranged what the brothers of Joseph had ruled concerning the thief, in order to bring Joseph to his aim, out of His mercy and grace. In this there is an indication that Joseph did not overstep the king's law, for otherwise he would have acted arbitrarily as he willed; and this is from the abundance of (p-3576) his intelligence and the perfection of his wisdom. It is cited as evidence for the permissibility of calling the laws of the religions of disbelief "dīn" (religion), and the verses on this are numerous.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unless God willed﴾, it means that this matter occurred by God's will and arrangement, because all of that was an inspiration (ilhām) from God to Joseph and his brothers, until the matter proceeded according to what was intended.

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, that is, through knowledge, as We raised Joseph. The use of the imperfect form (present/future tense) indicates that this is a continuing divine custom (sunnah), not restricted to this case.

﴿And over every possessor of knowledge﴾, that is, of those who are raised, ﴿is One who knows﴾, that is, above him is one of higher rank than him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 77:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿They said, "If he steals, there has certainly stolen before him a brother of his." So Joseph kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, "You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you describe."﴾

﴿They said, "If he steals, there has certainly stolen before him a brother of his."﴾ This is a disclaimer from them to the Chieftain (al-'Aziz), by way of comparing him to [Joseph]. That is: this one has done just as a brother of his before him did, meaning by that Joseph.

﴿So Joseph kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, "You are worse in position"﴾ i.e., in standing (manzilah), in that you stole your brother from your father, then you proceeded to fabricate lies against the innocent.

﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you describe﴾ i.e., concerning the matter of Joseph.

The explanation of His words, may He be exalted:

﴿They said, "O chief minister, he has an elderly father of great age, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers."﴾

When it became certain that Binyamin would be seized and kept with Yusuf, in accordance with their own ruling, they began to appeal to his feelings by saying that he has an elderly father who loves him intensely and is consoled by him for his missing brother, so take one of us instead as a slave in your service.

Some scholars said: The jurisprudence (fiqh) to be derived from this sentence is that the elderly have a right by which one may seek a means of approach, just as they sought a means through Ya'qub's old age. It has also been reported regarding the prayer for rain (istisqa') that the elderly are brought out. End of quotation.

In what they resolved upon to rescue their brother from the bondage to which he had been condemned, there is evidence of good intention, fulfilment of promise, trustworthiness, true righteousness, and firm adherence to their father's covenant, in safeguarding his pleasure and honour. Thus should the dutiful one hold fast to the pleasure of his parents.

As for their words, ﴿indeed, we see you are among the good-doers﴾, the meaning is: toward us, so complete your kindness with this final act. Or it means: among those who are accustomed to doing good, so let this also come from you.

The discussion of the words of the Exalted:

[79] ﴿He said: "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property; indeed, then we would be wrongdoers."﴾

﴿He said: "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property; indeed, then we would be wrongdoers."﴾ That is: taking an innocent person in place of the accused is wrongdoing, because no one is to be seized for the crime of another. Some of them said: except what is related concerning the (blood-money of the) ʿāqila (the paternal kinsmen who bear the compensation).

And the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 80:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew apart, conferring privately. The eldest of them said, "Did you not know that your father has taken from you a solemn pledge in the name of Allah, and before this you failed in regard to Joseph? So I will never leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me, and He is the best of judges."﴾

﴿So when they despaired of him⦆ i.e., they despaired of Joseph and of his answering them, with the utmost despair, as indicated by the (sin and ta') [in istay'asu], for they are added for emphasis.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This degree of despair arose in them because they witnessed his seeking refuge in Allah from what they requested, which indicates that this matter is in the greatest degree of abhorrence to him, that it must be avoided, and that one seeks refuge in Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And [it is indicated] by his naming it (injustice) in His saying: ﴿Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers﴾ [Yusuf: 79]. And ﴿they withdrew apart﴾ (khalasu) means they isolated themselves and separated from the people, being alone, with no one else mixing with them. And (najiyyan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of the subject of ﴿khalasu﴾, meaning: they withdrew in this state, conferring privately. The circumstantial phrase is given in the singular although its subject is plural, either because (najiyy) is an adjective on the pattern (fa'il) meaning (mufa'il), like (ashir) and (khalit), meaning one who associates and mixes, as in His saying: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52], i.e., conferring; and this in usage is always used in the singular. One says: "They are your close associate (khalit) and companion (ashir)", i.e., those who mix with you and associate with you. Or because it is an adjective on the pattern (fa'il) like (sadiq) and its class, so it is given in the singular since it is in the form of verbal nouns, like (sahil), (wahid) and (dhamil). Or because it is a verbal noun meaning private conferring, applied to those conferring for the sake of emphasis, or because it is interpreted as a derived noun or verbal noun, and in its original sense it includes the few and the many; and treating the verbal noun as an adjective is more eloquent in meaning. This is why al-Zamakhshari said: "Better than it" — i.e., better than interpreting ﴿najiyyan﴾ as "possessors of private conference" or "a group conferring privately", i.e., conferring — "is that they were wholly absorbed in private conference, due to their gathering for it and their immersion in it with earnestness and concern, as if they themselves were the very image and reality of conferring; and their conferring was about arranging their affair — in what manner they would go, and what they would say to their father about their brother — like a people who have been overwhelmed by a calamity that befell them and so needed to consult." End of quote.

A subtle point:

Al-Qadi Iyad mentioned in (al-Shifa) in the section on the inimitability of the Qur'an that a Bedouin heard a man reciting: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew apart, conferring privately﴾ and said: "I bear witness that no created being is able to produce the like of this speech."

Al-Tha'alibi said in the book (al-Ijaz wal-I'jaz), in its first chapter: Whoever wishes to know the comprehensive words (jawami' al-kalim), to be alert to the excellence of brevity, to comprehend the eloquence of allusion, and to perceive the sufficiency of concision, let him ponder the Qur'an and reflect on its superiority over all other speech.

Then he said: Among that is His saying, Mighty is His mention, concerning the brothers of Joseph: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew apart, conferring privately﴾. This describes their withdrawing from all people, turning over opinions back and front, and their setting about fabricating what they would tell their father upon returning to him, and what accounts of the incident they would present to him. Thus those short words included the meanings of a long story.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The eldest of them said﴾ i.e., in age, as is the obvious meaning, and he, as is narrated, was (Reuben): ﴿Did you not know that your father has taken from you a solemn pledge in the name of Allah﴾ i.e., a firm covenant regarding returning your brother. It is attributed to Him, exalted is He, because the oath was sworn by His noble name. ﴿And before this﴾ i.e., before this [occasion] ﴿you failed in regard to Joseph﴾ i.e., you fell short concerning his matter. The (ma) is either superfluous and (min) is connected to the verb after it, and the clause is circumstantial; or it is a verbal (masdariyya) in the place of nominative by inception, with (min qabl) as its predicate, or in the place of accusative by coordination with the object of (ta'lamu). Or it is a relative (mawsula) in both cases, meaning: you put forward in his regard the betrayal, and did not keep your father's covenant after you said: ﴿And indeed we are to him sincere advisers﴾ [Yusuf: 11] ﴿And indeed we are to him guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 12].

﴿So I will never leave the land⦆ i.e., I will never depart from the land of Egypt ﴿until my father permits me⦆ i.e., to return ﴿or Allah decides for me⦆ i.e., to leave Egypt, or to free my brother by some means. ﴿And He is the best of judges⦆ because He judges only with truth and justice.

Then the eldest of them ordered that they inform their father of what had happened, and he said:

(p-3580) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[81] ﴿Return to your father and say, "O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we bear witness only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen."﴾

﴿Return to your father and say, "O our father, indeed your son has stolen"﴾ That is: he has been attributed to the theft of the king's bowl (ṣuwāʿ). ﴿And we bear witness only to what we know﴾ That is, we did not testify to him regarding the theft except by what we were certain of, namely the bringing out of the bowl from his baggage.

Admonition:

Some scholars have deduced from this that it is not permissible to testify to writing without knowledge and recollection. Likewise [it is not permissible] for one who hears someone's speech from behind a screen, since there is no knowledge of it—so it is in (al-Iklīl). It is not hidden that such a matter is one by which one may take support in the places of scholarly disagreement.

﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾ That is: and we did not know that he would steal when we gave you the solemn covenant.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 12, verse 82:

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[82] ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful.﴾

﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾ — they mean Egypt. That is: send to its people and ask them about the true nature of the matter. ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾ — that is, we came along with it. There had accompanied them a group from Canaan. ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ — that is, in what we have told you.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:**

﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you. So patience is beautiful. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾ [Yusuf: 83]

﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you"﴾ means: they returned to their father and told him what their brother had said to them. He said: "Rather, your souls made it attractive (sawwalat), i.e., adorned it and made it easy for you, a matter you then did."

(p-٣٥٨١) A subtle point:

Al-Zamakhshari said: "[It is] a matter you intended. Otherwise, how would that man know that the thief is seized for his theft, were it not for your fatwa and your instruction?!"

Al-Nasir said: "This is from al-Zamakhshari an anticipatory answer to an objection, as if a questioner were saying: 'In the first incident, their souls made a matter attractive to them without doubt. But in this second incident, they did not intentionally harm Benjamin, nor did they inform their father except with the reality in its clear form, and they left him in Egypt only because they were overpowered in taking him along. So what is the meaning of his saying a second time: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you﴾, as he had said to them the first time?' If the objection is raised on this basis, then the answer must be expanded. We say: At that time they were under suspicion in the eyes of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and they were deserving of his suspicion because of what they had previously done to Yusuf, peace be upon him. There was also a circumstantial indication that affirmed the negation of the accusation and strengthened it, namely the king's seizing him for theft. This was not from the religion (din) of Ya'qub alone, not from the religion of other people, nor from their custom. To this the Exalted's words allude: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yusuf: 76], as a warning from Allah, the Exalted, to the manner in which Ya'qub suspected them. So he knew that the king had only done this by their fatwa to him, and he thought that they had issued that fatwa to him after the theft became evident, deliberately, so that their brother would be left behind.
