In reality, they had been asked for a ruling before the king claimed the theft against them, so they mentioned what they had, and they did not realize that the aim was to hold them to what they had said. Accusing someone who is in a position where suspicion may fall upon him is not blameworthy, especially concerning what concerns a father from a son. It is possible—and Allah knows best—that the reason which permitted him to say this about them is that they made the mere presence of the goblet in the baggage of whoever was found with it a theft, without referring the judgment to establishing with a known basis that he was a thief. This, in our sacred law (shar'), does not establish theft against him—and Allah knows best."

His words: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you﴾ are placed in their proper context of their condition, even though their law (shar') requires that matter differently from our law. The principal answer is the first one. End.

(p-٣٥٨٢) And His words, the Exalted: ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, i.e., without anguish. ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, i.e., Yusuf and his brother who was held in Egypt, so that his sorrows will depart all at once. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾, i.e., All-Knowing of my condition and their condition, All-Wise in intensifying the matter so that He may see the measure of patience, and reward will be poured out according to its measure. Among the reward that comes quickly is the hastening of relief.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[84] ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from the grief, and he was suppressing (his anger).﴾

﴿And he turned away﴾ i.e., he turned away from them, ﴿from them﴾ i.e., from his sons, out of aversion to what they had brought. ﴿And said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ i.e., O my intense sorrow. The alif (in "yā asafā") is a replacement for the ya' of the first person, for lightness. It was also said that it is the alif of lamentation (nudbah), with the ha' omitted. The (asaf) is the most intense grief and regret over what has passed. He grieved over Joseph alone, not over his two brothers, although the event afflicted all three. A more recent calamity is more severe upon the soul and has a more visible effect, because the calamity of Joseph was the foundation of his misfortunes, upon which the other calamities that befell his son were built. So his grief over him was grief over whoever was joined to him. Also, because it had not left his thought, it remained fresh and tender with him, as it has been said:

"The most grievous of calamities did not make me forget his absence, and every new thing reminds one of the old."

And also because he was confident of their lives, but not of his.

﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾, and that was due to the abundance of his weeping.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When weeping is abundant, the tears wear away the blackness of the eye and turn it to a dull whiteness. ﴿And he was suppressing (his anger)﴾, i.e., filled with rage over his sons, yet he did not show what would grieve them. (Fa'il) is in the sense of (maf'ul), as in His saying: ﴿and he is full of suppressed anger﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], or it means one who swallows anger or grief intensely, because he never complained of it to anyone; so it is in the sense of (fa'il).

A note:

The verse indicates the permissibility of expressing grief and weeping at calamity.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: How was it permissible for the Prophet of Allah to reach such a degree of distress?

I say: Man is created such that he cannot control himself in the face of severe grief, and for this reason his patience is praised, and that he restrains himself so that he does not go to what is not becoming.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept over his son Ibrahim and said: "The eye sheds tears and the heart grieves, and we say nothing except what pleases our Lord, and indeed we are saddened by your separation, O Ibrahim."

The blameworthy distress is only that which proceeds from the ignorant: shrieking, wailing, striking the chest and face, and tearing garments.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that he wept over a son, or someone else, and was asked about it, and he said: "I have not seen Allah make grief a shame upon Ya'qub."

And His Exalted saying:

(p-٣٥٨٤) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[85] ﴿They said, "By God, you will not stop remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become among those who perish."﴾

﴿They said﴾, i.e., the sons of Ya'qub said to their father, in a manner of gentleness toward him and compassion for him: ﴿By God, you will not stop remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill﴾, i.e., sick and close to ruin, ﴿or become among those who perish﴾, i.e., by death. They mean: if this state continues for you, we fear for you destruction and loss. It was cited as evidence for the permissibility of swearing on the basis of strong conjecture (ghalabat al-zann). It was also said: they knew it, but they treated it as if it were something denied, and therefore they emphasized it.

And (tafta'u) is the present tense of fati'a, whose ta' may be vocalized in three ways. It is used with negation, either pronounced or implied, because its position is known, so it is elided for lightness, as in his saying:

"So I said, 'By God's oath, I will not leave off sitting beside you, even if they cut off my head and my limbs.'"

That is: I will not leave off. The meaning of (tafta'u) is: you will not cease and you will not depart.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[86] ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know."﴾

﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish"﴾, i.e., my distress and my condition. ﴿And my grief to Allah﴾, i.e., I do not complain to any one of you or to anyone else. I only complain to my Lord, calling upon Him and seeking refuge in Him. So leave me and my complaint.

﴿And I know from Allah﴾, i.e., for the one who complains to Him, that He can remove the complaint and increase the mercy, ﴿what you do not know﴾, i.e., what necessitates good opinion of Him. He is with His servant's opinion of Him.

When he knew of the severity of the trial together with patience, that relief was near, he strengthened their hope and commanded them to travel to Egypt and seek news of Yusuf and his brother, with his saying:

(p-3585) The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[87] ﴿O my sons, go and seek news of Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people.﴾

﴿O my sons, go and seek news of Joseph and his brother﴾ means: learn about their news and find out their condition. ﴿And do not despair of the mercy of God﴾ means: of His relief (faraj) and His mercy, which brings relief from hardship. ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God﴾ (it does not say "from Him," as an indication that its attainment is evident for the one who does not despair) ﴿except the disbelieving people﴾ means: those who disbelieve in God and in His mercy and His power to bestow relief after a period of hardship has passed, and in His custom of bestowing ease along with hardship, especially with regard to one who holds a good opinion of Him.

And His, the Exalted's, saying:

The Discussion of the Interpretation of His, the Exalted, Words:

[88] ﴿So when they entered upon him, they said: "O Chief Minister, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable."﴾

﴿When they entered upon him﴾ means: upon Yusuf, after they had returned to Egypt. Because it is understood from the context, he omitted mention of him for brevity. ﴿They said: "O Chief Minister"﴾ meaning: the powerful king, the one who is unapproachable. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾ meaning: hardship from the drought. ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise﴾ meaning: with a few dirhams in exchange for what we are seeking to purchase. They belittled the price and regarded it as insignificant, out of humility before the king's dignity and in order to draw out his compassion and tenderness. The original meaning of (tazjiyah, "pushing away") is to thrust or cast aside, so they used it as a metaphor for the little that is pushed away, out of disinclination toward it. Therefore, ﴿give us full measure﴾ means: complete and enlarge the measure for us with these meager dirhams, just as one would enlarge it with good dirhams. ﴿And be charitable to us﴾ meaning: by returning our brother, or by giving full measure, or by overlooking and accepting what is not counted as a true equivalent. ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾ meaning: He will grant them the best of rewards.

(p-3586) Remarks:

The first: The verse gives guidance to a noble etiquette, namely putting means before aims, for they are more successful in achieving them. This is what these people did: they presented the mention of their frail condition, their humble entreaty, and their belittling of the exchange, and they did not confront him abruptly with their need. This was so that it would serve as a means to fulfilling their desire, by arousing pity, stirring compassion and tenderness, and moving the chain of mercy, as we have previously mentioned. Thereupon he was softened toward them, and mercy toward them overcame him, so he could not restrain himself from making himself known to them, as will come.

The second: From the verse is derived the permissibility of complaining of need to one from whom its removal is hoped for.

The third: Some have cited His, the Exalted, words ﴿give us full measure﴾ as evidence that the wage of the measurer is upon the seller, since if the fulfilling of the measure is incumbent upon him, then its costs and whatever completes it are upon him.

The fourth: Some have cited His, the Exalted, words ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ as evidence for those who say that charity was not forbidden for the prophets (so stated in al-Iklil), and this is after granting that the brothers of Yusuf were prophets. There is disagreement on this. The verification of this will come in the remarks at the end of the surah.

The fifth: His, the Exalted, words ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾ are an exhortation to good deeds and an indication that the one who does good is rewarded with the best of rewards from Him, the Exalted, even if the one to whom good was done does not repay him.

Then He (Exalted) showed Yusuf's gentleness in making himself known to them, with His saying:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[89] ﴿He said, "Do you know what you did with Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾

﴿He said﴾ i.e., Yusuf, answering them: ﴿"Do you know what you did with Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ i.e., heedless youths? It is an interrogative of affirmation (taqrir), which conveys the magnitude of the event. Its meaning: how great is what you committed against Yusuf, and how vile is what you undertook! As one says to the wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed, and do you recognize whom you opposed?" And this verse confirms His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive."﴾ [Yusuf: 15]

Subtleties:

The first: Al-Mahayimi (al-Mahayimi) offered a wonderful connection in Yusuf's saying to them: ﴿Do you know﴾ following their saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88]. He meant, by their saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88], that He would give them in the Hereafter what is better than worldly compensation. So Yusuf indicated to them: "You want to avert the immediate harm by promising the deferred reward, and you do not avert from yourselves the deferred harm, as if you deny it. Do you know the harm of what you did to Yusuf?"

The second: It has been said that among his gentleness toward them is his saying: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾, as an excuse on their behalf; for committing an ugly act in ignorance of its ugliness is easier than committing it knowingly. Had they sought every avenue of excuse, they would not have found an excuse like this. Do you not see that Musa, peace be upon him, when he excused himself, said no more than: ﴿I did it then, while I was of the astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 20]? So there is in it a lightening of the matter for them.

The third: Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What was their act toward his brother?" I say: their exposing him to grief and bereavement, by separating him from his full brother (from the same father and mother), their harshness toward him, so that he could not speak to any of them except as the humbled speaks to the mighty, and their harming him with various kinds of harm. End.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[90] ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly favored us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient – then indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost."﴾

﴿They said﴾ – meaning: in astonishment and amazement, that this is something known only to Joseph: ﴿"Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ – meaning: the one whom you did what you did to. ﴿"I am Joseph, and this is my brother"﴾ – meaning: a full brother of mine from my two parents.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This added to them an emphasis in identifying himself, and an magnification of the status of his brother, and a completion of what his saying ﴿"Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?"﴾ [Yusuf: 89] conveyed, as indicated by his saying ﴿"Allah has certainly favored us"﴾. It is as if he said: "Do you know what you did to us of separation and humiliation? I am Joseph, and this is my brother, and Allah has certainly favored us with deliverance from what we were afflicted with, with reunion after separation, with honor after humiliation, and with intimacy after estrangement."

Then he gave the reason for that by way of a resumptive explanatory clause, with his saying ﴿"Indeed, whoever fears Allah"﴾ – meaning: fears his Lord in all his circumstances – ﴿"and is patient"﴾ – meaning: under adversity and against sins – ﴿"then indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost"﴾ – meaning: their reward. And placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun is a warning that those described with taqwa (God-consciousness) and patience are also described with ihsan (excellence).

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[91] ﴿They said: "By God, God has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners."﴾

﴿"By God, God has certainly preferred you over us"﴾ meaning: He has favored you over us by what you mentioned of piety (taqwa), patience (sabr), and the way of the doers of good (al-muhsinin). ﴿"And we were indeed sinners"﴾ meaning: and the case and condition of us was that we had deliberately committed the sin; we neither had taqwa nor did we have patience, so we did to you what we did, and for this reason you were preferred over us. In this is an indication of repentance (tawbah) and seeking forgiveness (istighfar), and for this reason:

The interpretation of His words, the Exalted:

[92] ﴿He said, "No reproach will there be against you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

﴿He said, "No reproach"﴾ — i.e., no censure, no rebuke, no reprimanding. ﴿"against you today"﴾ — i.e., even though you were blameworthy before the manifestation of the outcome of your deed, and there is no sin upon you; for ﴿"Allah will forgive you"﴾ — i.e., (He will forgive) my right, for my pleasure with you, and His right too, out of the vastness of His mercy, as He said: ﴿"and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful"﴾ — i.e., it is as if there were no error on your part. And (﴿today﴾) is connected to the reproach, or to what is implied in (﴿against you﴾) of the meaning of settledness. The meaning: "I will not reproach you today," and today is the day that is the object of reproach, so what then do you suppose of other days?! Thus his expressing it with (﴿today﴾) is not because reproach occurs on other days, for whoever does not reproach at the first meeting and the kindling of its fire, then after it is so by way of priority.

Al-Sharif al-Murtada said in (al-Durar): "Today" is placed in the position of the whole of time, as in his saying:

"Today, whoever used to envy us shows us mercy, and today we follow those who used to follow us."

Then he increased them in honour by invoking forgiveness for them, for what had passed from them, with his saying: ﴿"Allah will forgive you"﴾.

And his saying: ﴿"and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful"﴾ is a confirmation of the attainment of forgiveness, for he pardoned them, so Allah is more worthy of pardon and mercy toward them, and it is an indication of confidence in the answering of the supplication. It was also permitted for (﴿today﴾) to be connected to (﴿forgives﴾). The sentence is informative, brought as good news of Allah's swift forgiveness, because of their repentance and remorse for their error that renewed on that day. The first aspect is more apparent; the second is among the strained (i'rab) interpretations.

Note:

Some have said: Yusuf's overlooking the sin of his brothers, his sparing them, and his befriending them teach us that we should forgive those who wrong us, be kind to them, purify our love for them, and overlook every insult that befalls us; then Allah, Exalted, lavishes on us His blessings and goodness in this world, as He expanded provision for Yusuf, and bequeaths us eternal happiness. But if we harbour evil toward those who wrong us and seek vengeance against them, Allah will take vengeance on us and bring us to the place of destruction, so we seek refuge in Allah from the evils of our souls and the misdeeds of our actions.

Then Yusuf said to them:

(p-3590) The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, words:

[93] ﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. And bring me all your family.﴾

﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. And bring me all your family.﴾ Yusuf intended to give his father the good news that he was alive, to bring him joy by it, and to confirm this by sending a robe from his own robes, which he would wear or wrap himself in, to stand in contrast to the first shirt, which had brought grief and clouded the eye. The phrase "casting it over his face" means taking great pains to bring it close to him, because of the weakening of his sight, so that his strength of sight returns through the revival of his heart, by his smelling it and being reassured about his well-being. Joyful things have a great effect on bodily health and the strengthening of the organs. Dawud al-Antaki, the wise physician, discussed this excellently in his book *Tadhkira* under the entry on "joyful" (mufrih), in a way that one cannot do without consulting.

In *al-Kunuz* (Kunuz), one of the books of medicine, it is said: joy, if it comes gently, benefits the body, expands the soul, and refreshes the intellect, so the organs grow strong and revive. End of quote.

Then I saw that al-Razi relied on something close to what we have mentioned. His words are: The exegetes said: When Yusuf made himself known to them, he asked them about his father. They said: His eyes have gone blind. So he gave them his shirt. The verifiers said: He only knew that casting the shirt over his face would restore the strength of his sight through a revelation from God, Exalted is He; had it not been for revelation, he would not have known this, because reason does not indicate it. It may be said: perhaps Yusuf, peace be upon him, knew that his father had become blind only because of excessive weeping and constriction of the heart, which weakened his sight. So when his shirt was cast upon him, his chest must have been expanded and intense joy must have arisen in his heart, and this strengthens the spirit and removes weakness from the faculties. Then his sight is strengthened and that deficiency leaves him. This much can be known by the heart, and the medical laws indicate the soundness of this meaning. End of quote.

(p-3591) It is possible that al-Razi meant by "the verifiers" the Sufis, or those who stop at the outward meaning alone. It is not hidden that the style of the Revelation, in its metaphors and figures of speech, is a unique style, and one should be attentive to it.

In His words ﴿he will regain his sight﴾ (*ya'ti basiran*), it is permitted that its meaning be "he will become seeing" (yasir basiran), or "he will come to me seeing," taking *ityan* (coming) in its literal sense, so that *basiran* (بَصِيرًا) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). It has been said that His words ﴿And bring me all your family﴾ support this, meaning: with your father and others. There is room for doubt here, because the two verbs being identical in form does not show that they are identical in meaning. One cannot say that the basic principle is the literal meaning, because that applies only where the context requires it, and the context here does not require it. So the first reading is more delicate and more original, because of the sound-correspondence (tajanus) it contains.

It is reported that Yusuf, peace be upon him, after he had prayed for their forgiveness, said to them: God sent me ahead of you so that I might give you life. Two years of famine have passed in the land, and five years remain in which there is no plowing and no harvest. God sent me ahead of you so that He might leave you a remnant in the land and preserve you for a great deliverance. He, glorified is He, has made me a father to Pharaoh, a master over all his household, and one who holds power over the whole land of Egypt. So hurry and go to my father, and tell him of all my glory in Egypt and what you have seen. Say to him: "Thus says your son Yusuf: God has made me master over all the Egyptians. So come to me. Settle in the land of Goshen, and be near me, you and your sons and your sons' sons, your flocks, and all that is yours; I will provide for you here, for five years of drought remain, and I fear that the family and the property will perish." The news had reached the house of Pharaoh. It is also said that when Yusuf's brothers came, Pharaoh and his close circle were pleased by this. He also ordered Yusuf to insist that they bring their father and their families, and promised them the best land in Egypt to be theirs, so that they would not grieve over what they had left behind. Then Yusuf provided his brothers with the finest provisions, gave them a generous amount of robes, garments and dirhams, and sent the same to his father. He also sent them with carts for their children and women, and instructed them not to quarrel on the road. God knows best.

And His, the Exalted, words:

(p-3592) On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[94] ﴿And when the caravan departed, their father said: "Indeed I perceive the scent of Joseph, were it not that you think me senile."﴾

﴿And when the caravan departed﴾, i.e., it went out of Egypt. It is said: "al-qawm fasala 'an al-makan and infasalu" (the people departed from the place), meaning they separated from it. ﴿Their father said﴾, i.e., to his grandchildren and those around him from his people, out of the intensity of his longing for Joseph and his waiting for the mercy of God: ﴿Indeed I perceive the scent of Joseph, were it not that you think me senile.﴾ The "rih" (scent) is the fragrance that is found in a breeze. He was sniffing his fragrance coming toward him, a metaphor for his certainty of Joseph's existence, by what God had cast into his heart of his being alive, and of the glad tidings of his safety that came to him from the breezes of unseen good news. His hope in this from his Lord had grown greatly, and he was confident of attaining his desired aim and goal. For this reason he forbade his sons from despairing of the mercy of God. When the end of hardship draws near, the breezes of relief begin to blow, carrying the fragrance of ease. Everyone whose perception is strong, whose intelligence is great, and whose insight is illuminated knows this; he can almost touch the blossom of relief at the extreme of hardship, and he would not break his oath if he swore that he finds from its breeze the purest relief. Whoever knows, knows this; so much more fitting is it for those who have attained the summit of nobility through prophethood.

The attribution of "scent" to the son is well known in their speech. In a hadith in al-Tabarani: "The scent of a child is from the scent of Paradise." And the poet said:

Oh how lovely is the scent of a child, the scent of the rihan (sweet herb) in the land!

As for His words ﴿were it not that you think me senile﴾, it means: "unless you think me senile," or: "were it not for it (that), you would believe me." And (fannadahu) means he attributed to him "fanad", with two fathas. It is the weakness of judgment and intellect from old age and advanced years.

In al-'Inaya it says: It is derived from "fanad", which is a stone or rock, as if he made him a stone for the lack of his understanding, as the poet said:

If you have not loved and do not know what passion is, then be a stone, of dry hard rock, solid.

Then it was extended in usage, so it is said: "fannadahu" when one weakens his opinion, and blames him for what he did.

And His words, Exalted is He:

(p-3593) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[95] ﴿They said: "By God, you are surely in your old error."﴾

﴿They said﴾, that is, his grandchildren and those around him. ﴿"By God, you are surely in your old error"﴾, that is, you are surely in your departure from the former right course, through your excessive love for Joseph, your constant mention of him, and your hope of meeting him. They thought that he had died or been scattered, so reunion with him was impossible; and they described it as "error" because of how firmly and persistently he held to it.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[96] ﴿So when the bearer of good tidings came, he cast it over his face, and he regained his sight. He said, "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾

﴿So when the bearer of good tidings came﴾, i.e., the one who informed him of what would gladden him concerning the affair of Yusuf. ﴿He cast it over his face﴾, i.e., the bearer of good tidings threw the shirt over the face of Ya'qub, or Ya'qub himself cast it over his own face. ﴿And he regained his sight﴾, i.e., he returned to seeing, because of the joy and revival that occurred within him. ﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾, i.e., concerning the life of Yusuf and the bringing of relief. It is also permissible that ﴿Indeed I know﴾ be an independent statement. The thing said, "Do not despair of the mercy of Allah" [Yusuf: 87], applies if the address is to his sons; or ﴿Indeed I find the scent of Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 94] applies if the address is to his grandchildren and those around him.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[97] ﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we were sinners."﴾

﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we were sinners."﴾ The pronoun (ḍamīr) refers to his sons. They asked him to seek forgiveness for them for what had proceeded from them, or for his grandchildren and those with him, in response to their saying: ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ [Yusuf: 95]. The first is closer and more correct.

Since it is due to one who acknowledges his sin that he be pardoned and that someone ask forgiveness for him, he promised them that.

(p-3594) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[98] ﴿He said: "I shall ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

﴿He said: "I shall ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ That is: I shall supplicate to Him on your behalf, for He is the One who overlooks evil deeds, and the Merciful toward whoever repents.

Al-Mahayimi said: They mentioned the sins without mentioning Allah, out of greater concern for them, as though the consideration of His subjugating power had overcome them. And Ya'qub mentioned the Lord without the sins, since they have no weight in comparison to His mercy, by which He nurtured all things. End of quote.

This is one of the subtle refinements and beauties of the Revelation.

Notice:

It has been said: In these verses there is evidence for the permissibility of giving and receiving glad tidings of worldly matters, and for its being recommended, and for the permissibility of rejoicing at the attainment of worldly blessings. There is also evidence for postponing seeking forgiveness and supplication until a time which one considers to be more present of heart than others, or which is better and closer to being answered.

It has been narrated that he postponed the seeking of forgiveness until the pre-dawn (al-sahar). Dedicating virtuous times to seeking forgiveness and supplication is well known in the Sunnah, and from it is prescribed seeking forgiveness at the pre-dawn, after the prayers, and at the conclusion of the Hajj. Supplication during prostration, at the time of the adhan, between the adhan and the iqamah, and at the breaking of the fast is closer to being answered than other times.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[99] ﴿So when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself and said, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security."﴾

﴿So when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself﴾ refers to the arrival of Ya'qub (Jacob) and his family before Yusuf (Joseph). (p-3595) This was because they all set out together, departed from the lands of Kan'an (Canaan), and had their children and women mounted on the carts that Fir'awn (Pharaoh) had sent. They took their livestock and herds with them and descended into the land of Misr (Egypt). It is reported that they were seventy persons. Yahudha (Judah) went ahead to Yusuf to guide him to the land of (Jasan) (Goshen), so that they might settle there. Then Yusuf went out in his chariot and met his father in (Jasan). When Ya'qub came into view, he threw himself upon his neck and wept for a long time.

By "their entering upon Joseph" is meant their reaching his meeting place outside the city, and by "he drew his parents to himself" is meant that he embraced them, clasped them to himself, and took them along with him in his chariot. Some have said that by "his parents" he meant his father and his maternal aunt, because his mother Rahil (Rachel) had died while giving birth to his brother Binyamin (Benjamin). Treating the maternal aunt as if she were the mother is because she is like the mother in being the wife of the father, in standing in her place, and in being deserving of honour, just as the paternal uncle is treated as a father in His saying: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael) and Ishaq (Isaac)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133].

﴿And he said, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security"﴾ meaning: safe from the famine and from all kinds of hardship.

**Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[100] ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before. My Lord has made it true. And He was kind to me when He took me out of prison and brought you from the desert after Satan had caused discord between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾

﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾, meaning he seated them with him on his royal couch, honouring them. ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾, meaning his father and his remaining brothers, who were eleven, prostrated to him as a greeting (taḥiyya) and an honour. Prostration before the eldest was, among them, customary in the manner that greeting is customary among us.

﴿And he said, "O my father, this﴾, that is the prostration, ﴿is the interpretation﴾, that is the explanation, ﴿of my vision from before﴾, that is, [p. 3596] the one I saw in the days of my youth, which was the prostration of eleven stars, the sun and the moon. ﴿My Lord has made it true﴾, meaning: a truth corresponding exactly to what has actually occurred in sense perception. ﴿And He was kind to me when He took me out of prison﴾, meaning He delivered me from slavery and made the king obedient to me, entrusting to me the treasuries of the land. In speaking only of his coming out of prison, and not of the grandeur of the king's dominion and the magnificence of his affair, there is humility, and in mentioning the hardship that preceded it, there is a continuing expression of gratitude and a remarkable refinement of the self. In this there is also an allusion to the blessing of release from confinement. For, as ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said when he was imprisoned by al-Rashīd:

*How many a dwelling, which distress has covered over its people, and they have been given hateful names,*
*A dwelling where the base are feared and avoided, and where the dignity of the noble is diminished.*
*A villain speaks what he wishes, and you see no free man speaking with gentleness and modesty.*
*His cheek, unwilling to touch beauty, guards itself through silence and averting the gaze.*

And a poet among the prisoners said:

*We came out of this world while we were of its people, yet we are neither among the living in it nor among the dead.*
*When the jailer came to us one day on some errand, we were astonished and said: "This one has come from the world."*

It is reported of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, that he wrote on the door of the prison: "These are the abodes of affliction, the testing of friends, the gloating of enemies, and the graves of the living."

Many men of letters have tried to praise prison with the magic of their eloquence. ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm said:

*They said, "You have been imprisoned." I said, "My confinement does not harm me. What sword is there that is not kept in its sheath?*
*Have you not seen the lion, proud, keeping to his thicket, while the rabble of beasts wander about?*
*The full moon is overtaken by the waning, and then its nights are made clear, and it seems to be renewed.*
*Every state has its successor, and perhaps the hated thing will reveal to you what you praise.*
*Prison, so long as one is not driven into a shameful baseness, is a fine lodging, a place of rest.*
*It is a house that renews the honour of the noble; he is visited in it and does not visit, and he is served."*

The finest thing said in consoling prisoners is the saying of al-Buḥturī:

*Is there not in the Messenger of God Yūsuf an example for one like you, imprisoned for injustice and falsehood?*
*He maintained beautiful patience in prison for a while, and then that beautiful patience brought him to kingship.*

Al-Tha'ālibī transmitted it in *al-Laṭā'if wa'l-Yawāqīt*.

﴿And he brought you from the desert﴾, that is, the badia, and they had been owners of livestock, ﴿after Satan had caused discord﴾, that is, corrupted, ﴿between me and my brothers﴾, that is, through envy. He attributed it to Satan because it came about through his whispering and his instigation. In this there is also a tactful avoidance of rebuking them. He mentioned it because a blessing after trial is more beautiful in its effect.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, meaning subtle in the management of it and gentle in dealing with it, ﴿indeed, He is the All-Knowing﴾ of the aspects of the benefits, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in His acts and decrees.

The commentary of the verse concerning His saying, Exalted is He:

[101] ﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me some of the kingdom and taught me something of the interpretation of events. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die in submission, and join me with the righteous.﴾

﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me some of the kingdom﴾ meaning a great portion of it, namely the kingdom of Egypt. ﴿And taught me something of the interpretation of events﴾ meaning the interpretation of dreams. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ meaning their Innovator and Creator. ﴿You are my Guardian﴾ meaning the Master of my affairs, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die in submission and join me with the righteous﴾ meaning among the prophets and messengers. Yusuf, peace be upon him, made this supplication when God's favor upon him had been completed through his reunion with his parents and brothers and through what He had bestowed on him of knowledge and kingship. So he asked his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that just as He had completed His favor to him in this world, He would preserve it for him for the rest of his life, and when his term drew near, take him in a state of Islam and join him with the righteous. There is therefore in it no wish for death, and the request for death to be granted immediately, as has been said, is not what is meant.

Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Let none of you wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he is a doer of good, he will increase in good; and if he is a doer of evil, perhaps he will repent. But let him say: O God, keep me alive as long as life is better for me." In another narration: "And cause me to die when death is better for me."

Two points:

First: Concerning the jurisprudence (fiqh, understanding of the legal rulings) of these verses: some of the Yemenis said: From what is related, that Yusuf went out to meet his father, one may infer the excellence of showing honor by going out to meet someone. Similarly the same applies to seeing a guest off, and from this is what is related concerning seeing off a guest. One may also infer, from what is related that the intended meaning of "his mother" was his maternal aunt, as has passed, that whoever attributes a man to his maternal aunt, saying "O son of so-and-so (a woman)!", is not slandering her. And one may infer from their (his parents') being raised upon the throne, which is the high couch, the permissibility of making it and of raising others up to honor the one who is raised. One may also infer from His saying: ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾ [Yusuf: 100] that moving away from the desert is a blessing, because of the coarseness that befalls the people of the desert, and their remoteness from the sources of knowledge, from the refinements of urban life, the gentleness of social intercourse, and human perfections. It is related that Jarir said:

"The land of tillage: if Jarwal came to it, meaning al-Hutay'a, he would become a farmer.
Whatever way you came to its houses, you would think them graves."

In the hadith: "Whoever lives in the desert becomes coarse," meaning whoever dwells in the desert. And in another: "Coarseness and hardness are among the owners of the fadaddin (the sheep and camel herders in the far desert)." In this there is evidence for the goodness of moving from the deserts to the cities. End of quotation, with additions.

Second: Many have recounted the account of Ya'qub and his family settling in Egypt. Its summary is that Yusuf chose for them the land of Jasan (Goshen) as their dwelling. When they entered Egypt, Yusuf informed Pharaoh of the arrival of his father, his brothers, and all their possessions in the land of Jasan. Then he brought his father before Pharaoh, who honored him and spoke with him at length. He asked him his age, and he replied: a hundred and thirty years. Pharaoh granted him and his sons the best land in Egypt, which is the land of Ramesses, that is, 'Ayn Shams, and made it their possession. Ya'qub prayed for him and then departed. Then Yusuf took five of his brothers and set them before Pharaoh, who said to them: "What is your trade?" They answered him, as Yusuf had instructed them: "We and our fathers are shepherds of sheep!" Pharaoh said to Yusuf: "If you know that among them are people of skill, then appoint them as overseers of my livestock." Yusuf allotted provision of food for his father, his brothers, and the rest of his family according to their needs. They settled in the land of Egypt at Jasan, and they acquired property there, multiplied, and became exceedingly numerous. Ya'qub lived in the land of Egypt for seventeen years, so the whole span of his life was a hundred and forty-seven years. When his end drew near, he said to Yusuf: "Do not bury me in Egypt when I die, but carry me from it to the burial place of my fathers," and Yusuf agreed to this. Then after a period, Yusuf was informed of his father's illness, so he took his two sons and set out to his father. His father revived at his arrival and saw his two sons, and said: "Who are these two?" He said: "My sons, whom God has granted me here." He said: "Bring them near to me," so he brought them near, and he kissed them and prayed for them, and said to him: "I never thought I would see your face, and now God has shown me your offspring also." Then he informed Yusuf of the approach of his death, and gave him the good news that God would be with you (all) and would return you to the land of your fathers. Then he called the rest of his sons, prayed for them for blessing, and enjoined them to take him up to his people and to bury him with his fathers in the cave that is in Hebron, which is known today as the city of al-Khalil, for in it were buried Abraham and Sarah his wife, Isaac and Rebecca his wife, and Leah the wife of Ya'qub. When Ya'qub had finished his counsel to his sons, his soul departed, and Yusuf fell upon his father's face, wept, and kissed him. Then he commanded the physicians to embalm him and to preserve him. When the days of mourning for him had ended, Yusuf sought Pharaoh's permission to go out to bury his father, in fulfilment of his testament, and he granted him permission. He set out from Egypt, accompanied by his brothers, the family of his father, his retinue, the notables of Egypt, and Pharaoh's attendants, in a great procession, until they reached the land of Canaan. They buried him in the cave, as he had enjoined, and then returned with those who were with them to Egypt. Yusuf continued to care for his brothers with honor and kindness until his end drew near, and he enjoined them to carry him with them when they returned to the land which God had prescribed for their fathers. Then Yusuf died, at the age of a hundred and ten years, and they embalmed him and placed him in a coffin in Egypt.

This is what the early historians have related, and God knows best the realities. The Noble Qur'an did not mention this because the Qur'an was not built upon the canon of history. There is therefore in it nothing of history in the sense of mere narrative and reports. Rather, what it contains are signs and lessons, which appear within the context of events. For this reason a story is not related with its chronological order and details; rather the point of the lesson in it is mentioned, as will come with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111], and His saying: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud: 120]. The exposition of this discussion has passed in the introduction, so refer back to it. God willing, we will mention in the surah some of the wisdoms and lessons drawn from the account of Yusuf, so wait.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[102] ﴿That is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you (O Muhammad). You were not with them when they agreed upon their plan while they were scheming.﴾

﴿That is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾: a reference to what preceded of the story of Yusuf, whose perfection is far-reaching in all the countless excellences and secrets, to the point that it becomes a miracle. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: this is among the reports of the past unseen matters, which We reveal to you and inform you of, because of what it contains of admonition and moral lesson.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you were not with them when they agreed upon their plan while they were scheming﴾, it serves as evidence that it is an unseen report and a heavenly revelation. That is: you did not know this report except through revelation, because you were not present with the brothers of Yusuf when they agreed upon their plan to throw their brother into the well, while they were scheming against him, when they urged him to go out with them, plotting harm for him, and (scheming) against their father in asking his permission to send him with them. That is: you did not witness them, so that you could be acquainted with the outward and inward aspects of their secrets.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The intent is not merely the negation of his (peace be upon him) presence at the scene of their agreement and their scheming only, but at all the scenes as well. Its singling out for mention is because it is the starting point of the story and it conceals its circumstances, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they were scheming﴾ indicates. Although the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the intent is to put the deniers under obligation. The meaning: that is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, since there is no way for you to know it except that, for your not hearing it from others and your not studying books is a matter that the deniers also do not doubt. You were not among them at the time the matter occurred so that you could know it as it is and convey it to them. In this there is a mockery of the disbelievers, as though they doubt this, and so it repels their doubt. In it also is a notification that what has been mentioned of the report is the truth that corresponds to reality, and what the People of the Book transmit is not as it really is. That is: such verification without revelation is conceivable only through presence and witnessing, and since there was no such presence, it is by revelation. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, (to see) which of them would take charge of Maryam﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 44], and His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 44]. End.

His saying, exalted is He:

(p-3602) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[103] ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should strive eagerly, will not be believers.﴾

﴿And most of mankind﴾: He intends by this the generality [of people], or the people of Makkah. ﴿Even if you should strive eagerly﴾, meaning: you exert every effort upon their faith and go to great lengths in displaying the decisive signs that indicate your truthfulness. ﴿Will not be believers﴾, meaning: in the Books and the Messengers, because of their inclination toward disbelief and the path of evil. The meaning is: by means of this account, his prophethood, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, has already become clear and the proof has been established. Yet despite this, most of mankind did not believe, as Exalted Allah said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾.

Al-Razi said, in substance: The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that the disbelievers of Quraysh and a group of the Jews asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, to recount the story of Yusuf out of obstinacy. It was thought that they would believe when it was recited to them. When it was revealed and they persisted in their disbelief, it was said to him: ﴿And most of mankind…﴾ etc. It seems to be an allusion to what is mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56].

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[104] ﴿And you do not ask them any reward for it. It is not but a reminder to the worlds.﴾

﴿And you do not ask them any reward for it﴾ — i.e., for this advice and this calling to what is good and right guidance. ﴿Any reward﴾ — i.e., any wage. ﴿It is not but﴾ — i.e., it is not, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿A reminder to the worlds﴾ — i.e., an admonition for them, through which they may be mindful, be guided, and be saved in this world and the Hereafter. The meaning is that this Qur'an contains far-reaching admonition and upright guidance, and you do not seek from them, in reciting it to them, any wealth or payment. So if they were people of intellect, they would accept it and would not rebel.

Some of the Yemenis said: The verse is evidence that whoever takes on the role of guiding people, whether through teaching or admonition, must avoid whatever would prevent his words from being accepted.

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, statement:

[105] ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they turn away from it.﴾

﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they turn away from it.﴾ That is: how many a sign there is of the Creator's oneness, His overwhelming power, and His sublime attributes, in the heavens, from their stars and their spheres (aflak), and on the earth, from adjoining tracts of land, gardens and orchards, firm mountains, surging seas, vast deserts, animals and plants, various fruits, and living and dead things. They see them, yet they do not take heed from them.

Al-Razi said: This means that it is no wonder if they do not reflect upon the proofs that point to your prophethood, for the world is filled with proofs of tawhid (divine oneness), power, and wisdom. Then they pass by them and do not pay them any attention. Know that the proofs of tawhid, knowledge, power, wisdom, and mercy must necessarily come from perceptible things, and these are either the celestial bodies or the elemental bodies.

As for the celestial bodies, they are of two kinds: spheres and stars. As for the spheres, their specific measurements may be used as evidence for the existence of the Creator. Their being above or below one another may also be used as evidence. And their movements may be used as evidence, either because their movements are preceded by non-existence, so there must be a capable mover, or because of the manner of their movements in speed and slowness, or because of the difference in the directions of those movements. As for the stellar bodies, sometimes the existence of the Creator is proven by their measurements, their positions, and their movements; sometimes by their colors and their lights; and sometimes by their effects in producing light and shadows, darkness and brightness.

As for the proofs drawn from the elemental bodies: they are either drawn from simple (elemental) substances, which are the wonders of land and sea, or from compounds (mawalid), which are of several kinds:

(p-3604) The first of them: the upper phenomena, such as thunder, lightning, clouds, rain, snow, wind, and the rainbow.

The second: minerals, with their varying natures, properties, and conditions.

The third: plants, and the special qualities of wood, leaves, and dates, and the particularity of each of them with a specific nature, a specific taste, and a specific property.

The fourth: the variation in the states of animals in their shapes, natures, voices, and creation.

The fifth: the dissection of human bodies, the dissection of human faculties, and the explanation of the benefit obtained from them.

These are the comprehensive proofs.

From this same category also are the stories of the ancients and the accounts of the earlier peoples, and that kings, when they seize control of the earth, ruin the lands and subdue the servants, die, and nothing remains of them in this world, neither news nor trace, while the burden and the punishment remain.

Since human reason cannot encompass a full explanation of the proofs of the higher and lower worlds, they have been mentioned in the Noble Book in summary form. End.

And His, the Exalted's, statement:

The discussion of the words of the Most High:

[106] ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they associate others with Him.﴾

﴿And most of them do not believe﴾ — i.e., the people, or the people of Makkah — ﴿in God﴾ — i.e., in their acknowledgment of His existence and His being the Creator — ﴿except that they associate others with Him﴾ — i.e., by their worship of other than Him, by their taking the rabbis and monks as lords, and by their saying that God has taken a son. Glory be to Him, far exalted above what they say, with a great exaltation.

Notice: Just as the verse indicates the reproach against them for the greater shirk (shirk al-akbar), which is that others are worshipped alongside God, it also points to (p-3605) what permeates hearts and in which most people are immersed of hidden shirk (al-shirk al-khafi), of which its doer is generally unaware. Among the statements on this verse is that of al-Hasan: "That is the hypocrite, who acts when he acts for the show of people, and he is a associator (mushrik) by his deed," meaning: shirk in worship. Its possessor, although he believes in God's oneness, does not sincerely devote his servitude to Him, but rather acts for the sake of his own portion, or the pursuit of worldly gain, or the pursuit of rank, status and standing among creatures. So for God there is a share of his deed and effort, for his self, his portion and his desire there is a share, for Satan there is a share, and for creatures there is a share. This is the state of most people, and it is the shirk of which the Prophet ﷺ said, as narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih: "Shirk in this nation is more hidden than the crawling of an ant." Thus all showing-off (riya') is shirk; it nullifies worship, voids the reward of the deed, and one is punished for it if the deed was obligatory. For He, the Most High, commanded that He be worshipped sincerely. He said, the Most High: ﴿And they were only commanded to worship God, sincere to Him in religion, upright﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. Whoever does not sincerely worship God has not done what he was commanded, but rather what he did is something other than what was commanded, and so it is not accepted from him.

Muslim and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God says: I am the most independent of partners from shirk. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I leave him and his shirk."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid, traced back to the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed the thing I fear most for you is the lesser shirk!" They said: "What is the lesser shirk, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Showing-off (riya')."

Among shirk there is a type that is not forgiven, which is associating others with God in love and veneration, by loving a creature as one loves God. This is the shirk of which God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides God, equals﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], and so on. And the people of this shirk said to their gods, when they had been gathered into the Hellfire: ﴿By God, we were certainly in manifest error﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 97] ﴿when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 98]. It is known that they did not equate them with Him, glory be to Him, in creating, providing, causing death and life, dominion and power; rather they equated them with Him in love, deification, submission to them and humbling before them. This is the utmost ignorance and wrongdoing. How can one who was created from dust be equated with the Lord of lords? How can slaves be equated with the Owner of necks? How can the poor in essence, the weak in essence, the powerless in essence, the needy in essence, who has from his own self nothing but non-existence, be equated with the Rich in essence, the Capable in essence, whose richness, power, dominion, existence, benevolence, knowledge, mercy and absolute, complete perfection are necessary attributes of His essence? What injustice is more ugly than this, and what judgment is more grossly unjust than this, in that one who has no justice makes equal to His creation? This was conveyed by Shams Ibn al-Qayyim in (al-Jawab al-Kafi).

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: There is also a hidden shirk, of which its doer is generally unaware, as was narrated from Hudhayfah that he entered upon a sick man and saw on his arm a thread, so he cut it off, then said: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they associate others with Him.﴾

And in a hadith: "Whoever swears by other than God has associated (ashraka)." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Umar, and he graded it hasan. And in the hadith narrated by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and others from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed incantations (ruqa), amulets (tama'im) and tiwalah are shirk." Imam Ahmad narrated it in a more detailed form from Zaynab, the wife of 'Abdullah, who said: "'Abdullah, when he came from some need and reached the door, would clear his throat and spit, out of dislike that we should rush into something he disliked. She said: He came one day and cleared his throat, and with me was an old woman reciting incantations for me against redness (of the eye), so I hid her under the bed. She said: He entered and sat beside me, and he saw a thread on my neck, and said: What is this thread? I said: It is a thread that has been recited over for me! So he took it and cut it off, then said: Indeed the family of 'Abdullah are too rich to need shirk. I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: 'Indeed incantations, amulets and tiwalah are shirk.' She said: I said to him: Why do you say this, when my eye was shedding tears, and I used to visit a certain Jewish man who would recite over it, and when he recited it, it would calm down?! He said: That is only from Satan; he would prod it with his hand, and when he recited, he would withhold from it. It would have sufficed you to say what the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Remove the harm, Lord of mankind, heal, for You are the Healer; there is no healing but Your healing, a healing that leaves no illness.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever hangs an amulet has associated (ashraka)."

He also reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever is turned back from his need by omen (tiyarah) has associated (ashraka)."

From what has been mentioned, it is known that the wording of the verse encompasses everything to which the designation of faith truly applies, together with the existence of the designation of shirk. So the people of the greater shirk: most of them do not believe that God is the Creator except that they associate others with Him, by what they take as intercessors and what they worship of idols. Likewise the people of the lesser shirk among the Muslims, such as showing-off for example: most of them do not believe in God except that they associate others with Him in that hidden shirk. In light of this, shirk coexists with faith, for the one described by both of these, as mentioned, is a believer in what he believes, and an associator in what he associates. The naming in the Sharia belongs to God, the Mighty and Majestic, and to His Messenger, so they may apply whatever name they wish to whatever named thing they wish. Just as faith (iman) in language means assent (tasdiq), then God, the Mighty and Majestic, applied it in the Sharia to all acts of obedience and abstaining from sins (p-3608) when all of that is intended, whether action or abstention, for the face of God, the Most High; likewise shirk was transferred from associating something with another in general to associating in His worship, and in the special attributes of His lordship.

Ibn al-Qayyim said:

The reality of shirk is assimilating the created to the Creator, and assimilating the created to Him. The associator makes a creature resemble the Creator in the specific attributes of divinity. Among the specific attributes of divinity is sole possession of harm and benefit, giving and withholding, and this necessitates hanging supplication, fear and hope, and reliance upon Him alone. Whoever attaches these to a creature has made it resemble the Creator, and has made one who possesses for himself neither benefit nor harm, nor death nor life nor resurrection, much less for others, a likeness to the One to whom all command belongs, exalted is He. Among the most ugly of comparisons is the comparison of this powerless one, poor in essence, to the Capable, Rich in essence. Among the specific attributes of divinity is absolute perfection from all aspects, in which there is no deficiency in any respect. This necessitates that all worship be for Him alone: veneration, exaltation, awe, supplication, hope, turning in repentance, reliance, seeking help, and utmost humility together with utmost love; all of this is required by reason, Sharia and innate nature to be for Him alone, and it is prohibited by reason, Sharia and innate nature that it be for another. Whoever gives any of that to another has assimilated that other to One who has no likeness and no equal, and that is the most ugly and most baseless comparison. Because of its great ugliness and its embodying the utmost wrongdoing, God, glory be to Him, informed His servants that He will not forgive it, though He has prescribed mercy upon Himself. Among the specific attributes of divinity is servitude (ubudiyyah), which stands on two legs, and has no establishment without them: utmost love, together with utmost humbling. This is the completeness of servitude, and the ranks of creatures in it vary according to their variance in these two foundations. Whoever gives his love, his humbling and his submission to other than God has assimilated that other to Him in His pure right, and this is something impossible for any Sharia to bring. Its ugliness is fixed in every innate nature and intellect, but the devils have altered the innate natures and intellects of most creatures and corrupted them for them, and whoever had the good ending from God remained upon the innate nature. Having known this, among the specific attributes of divinity is prostration; whoever prostrates to other than Him has assimilated the created to Him. Among them is reliance; whoever relies upon other than Him (p-3609) has assimilated that other to Him. Among them is repentance; whoever repents to other than Him has assimilated that other to Him. Among them is swearing by His name in veneration and exaltation; whoever swears by other than Him has assimilated that other to Him. This is regarding the side of assimilation. As for the side of assimilating oneself to Him: whoever magnifies himself and exalts himself, and calls people to praise him with eulogy, veneration, submission, hope, and the hanging of the heart upon him, in fear, hope, seeking refuge, and seeking help, has assimilated himself to Him and disputed with Him in His lordship and divinity, and he deserves to be humiliated to utmost humiliation and abased to utmost abasement.

In the Sahih, from him ﷺ, he said: "God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: Greatness is My waist-wrapper and pride is My cloak; whoever disputes with Me one of them, I will punish him." Likewise whoever assimilates himself to Him in a name that is not fitting except for God alone, such as "King of kings," "Judge of judges," and the like.

In the Sahih, from him ﷺ: "The most hated man before God is a man called King of kings; there is no king but God."

This is God's anger against whoever assimilates himself in a name that is fitting only to Him. He, glory be to Him, alone is the King of kings; He judges over them all, and decides over them, and none other.

The continuation of this discussion is in Ibn al-Qayyim's (al-Jawab al-Kafi), so refer to it.

And the words of the Most High:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil, "The Beauties of Interpretation") on surah 12, verse 107:**

(p-٣٦١٠) The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning explanation of the meaning) of His saying, exalted is He:

[107] ﴿Do they then feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming punishment from Allah, or that the Hour will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive?﴾

﴿Do they then feel secure﴾: that is, these polytheists. ﴿That there will not come upon them an overwhelming punishment from Allah﴾: that is, a punishment that spreads over them and covers them. ﴿Or that the Hour will come upon them suddenly﴾: that is, unexpectedly. ﴿While they do not perceive﴾: that is, its coming. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do those who plot evil deeds feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will not come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ [An-Nahl: 45] ﴿Or that He will not seize them in their going back and forth, so they cannot escape?﴾ [An-Nahl: 46] ﴿Or that He will not seize them through gradual wasting? Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ [An-Nahl: 47] And His saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are sleeping?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 97] ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the morning while they are playing?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 98] ﴿Do they then feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 99]

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[108] ﴿Say, "This is my way. I invite to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me. And exalted is Allah; and I am not of those who associate others with Allah."﴾

﴿Say, "This is my way"﴾ That is, this is the path, which is the call to faith and monotheism. "My way" means my road, my course and my sunnah. The words sabil (path) and tariq (road) may be used in both the masculine and feminine. Then he explained his way with His words: ﴿I invite to Allah﴾, that is, to His religion and His monotheism, and to knowledge of His attributes of perfection and the descriptions of His majesty. ﴿With insight﴾, that is, with clear proof, not blind. ﴿I and whoever follows me﴾, that is, who has believed in me, also invite to Allah with insight, not on the basis of desire. ﴿And exalted is Allah﴾, that is, I glorify Him, honor Him and sanctify Him above having any partner, rival, equal, son or consort. He is exalted far above that, to a great degree. ﴿And I am not of those who associate others with Allah﴾, that is, I am not upon their religion.

Remarks:

First: As-Samin said: "﴿I invite to Allah﴾ may be a resumed (independent) clause, which is the apparent reading, or it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the speaker (ya'). And ﴿with insight﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of 'I invite' — that is, I invite while being upon insight. His words ﴿and whoever follows me﴾ are conjoined to the subject of 'I invite', and for this reason the independent pronoun was used for emphasis. It may also be a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, meaning: and whoever follows me also invites. It may also be that ﴿with insight﴾ is a predicate placed first, and 'I' (ana) is a delayed subject, and 'whoever follows me' is conjoined to it. The object of 'I invite' is either implied, meaning 'the people', or unmentioned."

Second: His words, Exalted is He, ﴿with insight﴾ indicate the distinction of this upright religion and its method, which stands alone, namely that it does not demand acceptance of it merely because it was brought by someone who narrates it. Rather, it makes claims, provides proof, relates the doctrines of its opponents and refutes them with argument, addresses the intellect, rouses thought, and presents the order of the universe and what it contains of precision and perfection to the examination of minds, requiring them to reflect deeply so that they may thereby reach certainty of the soundness of what it claims and calls to. See "The Treatise on Monotheism" (Risalat al-Tawhid) for the completion of this.

Third: The verse indicates that the conduct of the followers of the Prophet (ﷺ) is the calling to Allah.

Al-Razi said: Everyone who mentions the proof and answers the doubt has called to Allah to the extent of his capacity. This indicates that calling to Allah is only good and permissible with this condition, namely that one be upon insight regarding what he says, and upon guidance and certainty. If he is not so, it is pure delusion. End of quote.

It is not hidden that calling to Allah is only through spreading the demands of the religion and publicizing its manners and teaching.

Some have said: It befits the scholar that, when he mixes and sits with the common people, his speech with them should concern the explanation of obligations and prohibitions, voluntary acts of obedience, and the mention of reward and punishment, for good deeds and bad. His speech with them should be in clear, near expressions that they know and understand, and he should increase explanation of matters which he knows they are involved in. He should not remain silent until they ask him about some knowledge while he knows they are in need of it and compelled to it, for his knowing that is itself a question from them in the language of their state. The common people have become overcome by laxity in the matter of religion, in knowledge and in practice, so it is not fitting for scholars to aid them in this by remaining silent about teaching and guiding them, lest ruin become general and calamity grow great. Rarely do you test a common person — and most people are common — without finding him ignorant of obligations and prohibitions, and of matters of religion of which ignorance is not permissible or excusable. If he is not found ignorant of everything, he is found ignorant of some. And if he knows some of it, you will find his knowledge of it to be knowledge heard from people's tongues; if you wanted to turn it into ignorance for him, you would do so with the least effort, for there is no root or soundness in what he knows. In sum, it is incumbent upon scholars to sit with people in knowledge, to speak to them of it and to spread it among them, and the scholar's speech with them should be on the matter for which they came, just as when they come for a marriage contract, his speech with them should concern the rights of women regarding dower, maintenance and living with them in kindness; or when they come for a sale, his speech should concern valid sales and their etiquette, the benefits of beneficial trade, and avoiding deceit and fraud, and so on. The scholar should not plunge with those who plunge, nor spend any of his time on other than upholding the religion. By remaining silent about reminder and teaching, corruption prevails and harm becomes general. There is no power and no strength except through Allah.

And His words, Exalted is He:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[109] ﴿We sent not before you any but men, to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns. Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then reason?﴾

﴿We sent not before you any but men, to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns﴾ — meaning: not angels from the people of the heaven. This is a refutation of the words of the polytheists: ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fussilat: 14]. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We sent not before you any of the messengers but that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20], and His saying: ﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal﴾ [al-Anbiya: 8], and His saying: ﴿Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9], and the verse.

He argued by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿men﴾, that no woman was included in the line of prophethood.

Al-Qura (the towns) is the plural of qaryah (town). It is, according to al-Qamus (the Dictionary), a congregational city (miṣr jāmiʿ); and according to Kifayat al-Mutahaffiz: the qaryah is every place to which buildings are joined and which has become a settled dwelling; and it applies to cities and other than them. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: What is meant by al-qura here is cities; that is, they were not from the nomadic dwellers of the desert, who are the coarsest of people in temperament and character. This is the familiar and known matter: that the people of cities are gentler in temperament and more refined than the people of their deserts, and the people of the countryside and villages are closer in condition than those who dwell in the deserts. For this reason He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The Arabs of the desert are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 97], and the verse.

Qatadah said: They were only from the people of the towns because they are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the villages (al-umur).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have they not travelled﴾, meaning: these deniers, ﴿through the land and seen﴾, meaning a looking of reflection, ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾, meaning: of the denying nations. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they might have hearts with which to understand?﴾ [al-Hajj: 46], and the verse. When they hear the report of that, they see that Allah destroyed the disbelievers and saved the believers. This was His, Exalted is He, custom with His creation. For this reason He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah﴾, meaning: those who avoid shirk and abominations, and believe in Allah, His messengers and His books.

Ibn Kathir said: That is, just as We saved the believers in this world, so also We have prescribed for them salvation in the Hereafter, and it is better for them than this world, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We shall help Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir: 51].

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ meaning: will you not use your intellects, so that you know that the Hereafter is better, or know how was the end of those (earlier nations).

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that the final outcome belongs to His messengers, and that His help comes to them when their people's denial persists, to strengthen his heart, peace and blessings be upon him. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[110] ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whoever We willed was saved. But Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people.﴾

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾ meaning: of their people responding. ﴿And thought﴾ meaning: knew and were certain, that is, the messengers. ﴿That they had been denied, Our help came to them.﴾ It is read (kudhdhibū), with a damma on the kaf and a shadda on the dhal, meaning: their people denied them in what they brought, because of the prolonged affliction upon them. It is also read with a damma on the kaf and without the shadda on the dhal (kudhibū). In that case, the pronoun in ﴿thought﴾ [al-Jinn: 7], according to what they chose, refers to the people. That is, they thought that the messengers had been denied, meaning, in what they had been promised of help.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the pronoun refers to the messengers. That is: they thought, when they were weakened and overcome, that God had failed to fulfil what He had promised them of help. He said: "They were human," and he recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. Scholars found this problematic in the report from Ibn ʿAbbas, and they offered several interpretations of his words.

(p-3615) Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant by the "thought" what occurs to the mind and passes through the heart, of doubts, whisperings and inner speech, as is characteristic of human beings. End of quotation.

It was also said: what is meant by their thought, peace be upon them, is that: exaggeration in delay and postponement, by way of metaphorical imagery (al-istiʿara al-tamthiliyya, a metaphor built on a comparison of whole scenes), in which the exaggeration of delay is likened to the thought of falsehood, on the basis that each of them entails the other, since the sought outcome does not follow. So what belongs to one of them is used for the other.

Al-Khattabi said: There is no doubt that Ibn ʿAbbas would not allow of the messengers that they could be lied about concerning the revelation, nor that they could doubt the truthfulness of the one who informs them. So his words are understood to mean that they, because of the prolonged affliction upon them, the slowness of help, and the intensity of their seeking the fulfilment of what they had been promised, imagined that what had come to them of revelation was a supposition of their own selves, and they suspected themselves of error in receiving what came to them of that. Thus the one to whom the verb is attributed is themselves, not the bearer of the revelation. And what is meant by "denied" is "mistaken," not literal lying, as one says: "Your own self has deceived you."

The hafiz Ibn Hajar said: This is supported by the reading of Mujahid: ((wa-ẓannū annahum qad kadhabū)) with a fatha on its first letter and without the shadda, meaning: they erred. And the subject of "thought" would then be the messengers.

Abu Nasr al-Qushayri said: It is not far-fetched that what is meant is that the thought occurred to the hearts of the messengers, but they turned it away from themselves. Or the meaning is: they came close to suspicion, as one says: "I reached the dwelling," when you have come close to it.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: Its aspect is that the messengers feared, after God had promised them help, that the help might fail to come, not out of suspicion about God's promise, but because of the suspicion of their own souls that they might have committed some act that breaks that condition. So when the matter lengthened and the affliction upon them intensified, the thought entered them from this direction.

Al-Wahidi related from Ibn al-Anbari that he said: What is related from Ibn ʿAbbas is not reliable, and it is not his speech; rather, it is to be interpreted in a way that agrees with it.

(p-3616) Ibn Hajar said: It is strange that Ibn al-Anbari was certain that it is not authentic, and then al-Zamakhshari hesitated about its authenticity from Ibn ʿAbbas, for it is authentic from him. Al-Bukhari related it in the tafsir of al-Baqarah with the wording: "He took it there," and he pointed to the sky.
